- **Off by default.** Without `MCP_REVIT_HTTP=1` no socket is created. A value other than `1`, `true`, `yes`, `on`, `0`, `false`, `no`, `off` or empty is refused at startup.
- **Loopback only.** The server binds `127.0.0.1`. `MCP_REVIT_HTTP_HOST` accepts only `127.0.0.1` and `localhost`; any other host, including `0.0.0.0`, stops the server with an error. The port is `MCP_REVIT_HTTP_PORT` (default 8765).
- **Required bearer token.** `MCP_REVIT_HTTP_TOKEN` must be set to at least 16 characters, otherwise the server does not start. Every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; a missing or wrong token gets `401` with the same body. The check uses `hmac.compare_digest` and runs on every path. The token is never logged or put in an error message. Generate one with `python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"`.
- **Host and Origin.** `Host` must be `127.0.0.1` or `localhost` (403 otherwise). An `Origin` header, when present, must be an `http` or `https` origin on `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` or `[::1]` (403 otherwise, including `Origin: null`). This blocks DNS rebinding and pages served from other sites. These checks run before the token check.
- **Approval gate unchanged.** Tools that change a model still need `plan_actions`, a human approval in the panel or with `aec-model-bridge-approve`, and `execute_plan`. The tools that approve, reject or roll back plans stay unreachable from MCP.

What it does not protect against:

- Other local users or processes that can read the token (the client's configuration or the process environment). Anything holding the token can call every tool the stdio server exposes, within the approval gate.
- Another local process that binds the port first. A client that sends the token to a port it did not start can leak it.
- Eavesdropping or tampering on the machine: traffic is plain HTTP on loopback and the token is not rotated.
- Remote access. Do not put this port behind a tunnel, reverse proxy or port forward.

### Panel HTTP shim (`panel_server.py`)
The panel hub (`aec-model-bridge-panel-server`, default port 8787) listens on `127.0.0.1` and serves `/execute`, `/agent/chat`, `/diagnostics`, `/reports`, `/agent/providers` and `/health`. Its only intended caller is the add-in's C# `HubClient`. Every request is checked:

- `Host` must be `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` (the port the hub is actually bound to), otherwise 403.
- Any request carrying an `Origin` header, including `Origin: null`, is refused with 403. `HubClient` sends no `Origin`.
- `POST` requires `Content-Type: application/json` (a `charset` parameter is accepted), otherwise 415.
- `OPTIONS` is not handled and no CORS headers are sent.
- `GET /health` returns only `{"status": "healthy"}` and needs no token. Every other route, including `/execute`, `/agent/chat`, `/diagnostics`, `/reports`, `/agent/providers` and unknown paths, needs the per-install token (next section).
- A `POST` body must be a UTF-8 JSON object of at most 1 MiB, nested at most 64 levels, with no `NaN` or `Infinity`. Otherwise the answer is 400 (413 when too large). On `/execute`, `arguments` must be an object; an unknown tool gets 400. A 5xx means a fault inside the hub. `tests/test_property_panel_execute.py` fuzzes these rules.

#### Panel hub token

The hub requires the header `X-AMB-Token` on every route except `GET /health`. A missing or wrong token gets `401` with the body `{"ok": false, "error": "Unauthorized"}`; the two cases are indistinguishable. The check is `hmac.compare_digest` and runs after the Host, Origin and Content-Type checks. Failed attempts are counted per hub process (20 per minute); past that, a failing request gets `429` without further work. A request with the right token is never counted or limited, so noise on the port cannot lock the panel out.

- **One secret per Windows user.** 32 random bytes (`secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`, 43 characters) in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AECModelBridge\panel-hub.token`, beside the add-in's `registry` folder. `MCP_PANEL_TOKEN_FILE` overrides the path.
- **The first hub to start creates it; everyone else reads it.** The file is written to a temp name with owner-only access and hard-linked into place, which fails if the name already exists, so two hubs starting together end up with one file and one token. Every later hub and every Revit's `HubClient` reads the same file, so all Revits sharing the hub use one token. The add-in never creates the file.
- **Owner-only.** On Windows the file's inheritance is removed and only the current user is granted access (`icacls`); if that fails, the hub does not start. On POSIX the mode is `0600`, and a file that is a symlink, owned by someone else, or accessible to group or others (any `0o077` bit) is refused with an error that names the file but never the token. Windows does not re-verify the ACL on read.
- **Never written elsewhere.** The token is not logged, not in audit logs, plans, proof bundles, diagnostics, chat or error messages. `redact_data` masks it by value and by the header name, and the hub's log file filter masks it as a second line of defence.
- **The page never sees it.** The panel's JavaScript does not call the hub. It posts messages to C# (`window.chrome.webview.postMessage`), and only `HubClient` calls the hub; a test checks that `panel/` contains no network calls and no reference to the token.
- **Rotation.** Stop every hub (end the `revit_mcp_server.panel_server` Python process), delete `panel-hub.token`, then start Revit. The next hub writes a new token. A running hub keeps the token it started with: if the file changes underneath it, the hub logs "token file changed ... restart the hub", and the panel, after one re-read of the file and one retry, shows "token changed" with the same instruction. An older hub (before this change) ignores the header; an older add-in talking to a new hub gets `401`. Update both together.

**Read-only reviewer credential (off by default).** A second secret lets a person or tool follow the queue without approval rights. It lives in `panel-reviewer.token` beside the panel token (`MCP_PANEL_REVIEWER_TOKEN_FILE` overrides the path), has the same format and owner-only file rules, and is created only by `python -m revit_mcp_server.security.panel_token --new-reviewer`. No MCP tool reads, creates or sets it. A client sends it in the header `X-AMB-Reviewer-Token` and the hub compares it with `hmac.compare_digest`. It is read when the hub starts; with no file, a malformed file, or a value equal to the panel token, reviewer access is off and the header gets `401`. A reviewer may call `GET /diagnostics`, `GET /reports`, and `POST /execute` with only `list_pending_plans` or `get_proof_bundle`. Every other route or tool, including approve, reject, rollback, execute, planning, `POST /approval-mode`, chat and unknown paths, gets `403`. If both headers are sent, a valid panel token wins; a wrong panel token is refused with `401` and counted as a failed attempt even when the reviewer header is valid. A reviewer's `instance` field is ignored, `/diagnostics` skips the write test, and `/diagnostics` and `/reports` leave out absolute workspace paths. The reviewer role is a read filter on the hub; it is not a second approver (see the two-person rule) and does not identify a person.

**What the token is, and is not.** It proves "a process running as this Windows user", and it keeps out browser pages (already blocked by the Host/Origin checks) and software that cannot read your profile. It does not by itself keep out another Windows user on a shared machine: that user could bind 127.0.0.1:8787 first and receive the token the add-in sends (see "Before any release: panel token and routing"; UNVERIFIED). It does not prove a person is present. Anything running as the same user, including an AI agent with a shell on your account, can read the file and call the hub. The real boundary is OS user separation plus the human-only approval flow: approving a plan from the panel is still recorded as `approved_via: "panel"` and the tool-call paths (MCP calls, the panel chat's tool calls, recipe steps, `execute_plan`) cannot reach `approve_plan`, `reject_plan` or `rollback_plan`. A command-line agent that can read files and open network connections as you can read the token file and call the hub directly; the hub launches `codex exec --sandbox read-only`, and whether that sandbox blocks reading the file or reaching loopback on Windows is UNVERIFIED. Run such agents with network access disabled where you can. Do not give an AI client a shell on the account you approve plans with. Other limits: the token travels over plain loopback HTTP, and any process that can read your user's files can read it.

#### Several Revits (instance routing)

One hub serves every open Revit. Requests that act on Revit carry an `instance` field, `{"pid": <Revit process id>, "document": <active document title>}`, which `HubClient` fills in from its own process. The hub looks the pid up in the live bridge registry (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\AECModelBridge\registry`, see [ADR 0014](adr/0014-multi-revit-routing.md)) and sends that request to that Revit's bridge; the endpoint and bridge token always come from the registry, never from the request. Without `instance`: a single live Revit is used; more than one is refused with `409` and a list of the live instances (pid, Revit year, start time). A pid with no live bridge is refused the same way. Only tools that read or decide on the hub's own plan files (`list_pending_plans`, `approve_plan`, `reject_plan`, `get_proof_bundle`) need no `instance`. `plan_actions` is not one of them: it reads before-values from Revit, so it is routed, or refused when the Revit is ambiguous. Module commands (recipe runner, warnings triage and the like) carry the routing into their worker threads and tool calls. Chat through the `claude` or `codex` command-line tool is refused while several Revits are open, because the CLI starts its own MCP server that cannot be pinned yet; the built-in assistant (API key) is routed for its tool calls (UNVERIFIED against a live Revit). The document title is shown for people only: the registry does not hold it, so it is not matched. Plans record the document and, when the add-in reports them, the Revit pid and start time (ADR 0017), so a recycled pid does not match a plan drafted in an earlier session (see "Before any release: panel token and routing"). UNVERIFIED against a live Revit.

What this does not do: it does not stop software running as the same user, and it does not change tool approval semantics; mutating tools remain gated by the approval flow.

### Panel HTTP shim (`panel_server.py`)
The panel hub (`aec-model-bridge-panel-server`, default port 8787) listens on `127.0.0.1` and serves `/execute`, `/agent/chat`, `/diagnostics`, `/reports`, `/agent/providers` and `/health`. Its only intended caller is the add-in's C# `HubClient`. Every request is checked:

- `Host` must be `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` (the port the hub is actually bound to), otherwise 403.
- Any request carrying an `Origin` header, including `Origin: null`, is refused with 403. `HubClient` sends no `Origin`.
- `POST` requires `Content-Type: application/json` (a `charset` parameter is accepted), otherwise 415.
- `OPTIONS` is not handled and no CORS headers are sent.
- `GET /health` returns only `{"status": "healthy"}`.

What this does not do: there is no authentication token yet, so it does not stop other software running as the same user from calling the port directly with a valid `Host` and no `Origin`. It does not change tool approval semantics; mutating tools remain gated by the approval flow. A token is planned separately.

---

## 3. Workspace sandboxing

All local file work (file reads, database exports, sheet prints) stays inside the configured directories.

### Configuration
Two environment variables control the sandbox:

| Environment variable | Python config field | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `MCP_REVIT_WORKSPACE_DIR` | `workspace_dir` | The default directory for generated files. Defaults to `~/Documents/AEC Model Bridge`. |
| `MCP_REVIT_ALLOWED_DIRECTORIES` | `allowed_directories` | A list of allowed directories, separated by semicolons (`;`). Defaults to the workspace directory only. |

### Enforcement
The `WorkspaceMonitor` class checks every path before any file operation:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from revit_mcp_server.security.workspace import WorkspaceMonitor

# Initialize with allowed paths
monitor = WorkspaceMonitor(allowed_directories=[Path("C:\\RevitProjects"), Path("C:\\exports")])

# Safe Path
safe_path = monitor.assert_in_workspace(Path("C:\\RevitProjects\\model.rvt"))  # Returns resolved Path

# Unsafe Path - Raises WorkspaceViolation
unsafe_path = monitor.assert_in_workspace(Path("C:\\Windows\\System32\\cmd.exe"))
```

### Client roots narrow the sandbox
When the MCP client declares the roots capability, the folders it has open (`roots/list`) narrow the allowed directories for that session. The effective set is the intersection of the configured directories and the roots. A root inside an allowed directory narrows to that root. A root that contains an allowed directory leaves it unchanged. A root outside every allowed directory is ignored and logged. Roots never add a directory. If the client declares roots and none overlaps an allowed directory, every tool that takes a path is refused with a plain message. A client with no roots capability, or an empty list, gets the configured directories unchanged. Only `file://` roots count; other schemes are ignored and logged. Roots are read once per session and again after `notifications/roots/list_changed`. If the client does not answer `roots/list`, the configured directories apply and a warning is logged. Plan, proof and reserved folders stay refused. Behaviour with real clients is UNVERIFIED. Code: `client_roots.py`, `security/workspace.py`.

### Path traversal guard
The `WorkspaceMonitor` turns each path into an absolute, canonical path. It then:
- Follows all symbolic links.
- Resolves relative parts (`..`, `.`).
- Checks that the result sits inside one of the allowed directories (`path.is_relative_to(allowed_dir)`).

---

## 4. Input validation and schema integrity

The server checks all tool arguments before it passes them to a provider.
- **Pydantic validation**: every MCP tool has a Pydantic schema. It sets the required parameters, data types and value limits.
- **Rejecting bad input**: the Python server rejects input that breaks the schema. Bad input does not reach the C# API thread.

---

## 4a. Plan approval: what is and is not protected

In Ask first mode, an AI assistant that wants to change the Revit model must draft a plan, and a person must approve it. Explicit Dev and Auto modes permit unplanned writes as described below; Look only refuses model changes.

### Protected

- **Humans approve.** `approve_plan`, `reject_plan` and `rollback_plan` are not listed to MCP clients and are denied to the panel's Claude chat. They are also refused on every internal path a model can reach: MCP calls, the panel chat, recipe steps and other module tool executors, `execute_plan`, and the approval provider's own tool entry point. A plan cannot contain one of them as an action. Only two routes run them: the panel route (`/execute` in the panel hub, recorded as `approved_via: "panel"`) and the command-line tool `aec-model-bridge-approve list | show <plan_id> | approve <plan_id> | reject <plan_id> | recover <plan_id>` (recorded as `approved_via: "cli"`; `recover` abandons stuck actions and does not approve anything). The panel has buttons for approve and reject, and the command line has no `rollback` command, so `rollback_plan` has no everyday route for a person yet; use Ctrl+Z or a revert plan (`plan_revert`, approved like any other plan).
- **Elicitation is never approval.** The server may ask the person a question through the AI client for a missing or ambiguous input (see `docs/elicitation.md`), but never for plan approval and never for secrets: the approval tools and the approval code cannot call the helper, and an answer only changes the arguments of a call that then goes through the gate as usual.
- **The route records the channel and the account.** `approved_via` is set by the code path and `approved_by` is the operating-system account that runs the panel hub or the command-line tool. Values a caller puts in the tool arguments (`approver`, `approved_via`) are ignored.
- **Plan ids are checked.** A `plan_id` must have the exact shape `plan_` plus 12 hex characters, and must resolve to a file directly inside `<workspace>/plans`. A plan file whose `plan_id` field differs from its file name is refused. A path, `../`, or any other shape is refused with a plain error.
- **An approval covers a hashed plan, and the command-line tool shows all of it.** When a plan is drafted, the server stores a content hash (`plan_hash`) of its id, creation time, snapshot id, skipped list, actions (tools, arguments, before values) and, when the plan carries one, its `review` block (summary, reasoning, citations, assumptions, elements left out, warnings) and `reverts_plan_id`. Plans with a review carry `hash_version: 2`; plans without one are hashed with the original rule and still verify. A plan that mixes the two (a review without version 2, or version 2 without a review) cannot be approved or executed. The review block is strictly validated (unknown keys, wrong types and over-long text are refused; total size is capped at 64 KB), stored as given and escaped when shown by `aec-model-bridge-approve show`. For large plans `show` and `approve` print the first 30 change rows and the first 300 characters of each value; `--all` prints everything, and `approve` refuses a plan whose review was cut short until it is run with `--all`, so a person approves only what they were shown. Anything else on a plan file is metadata that is **not hashed and not shown as approved content**: any extra key passed to `create_plan(extra=...)` (for example `reasoning` or a note), plus the lifecycle fields (`state`, `plan_hash`, `approved_*`, `rejected_*`, `executed_at`, `results`, `is_reversible`, `reversible_strategy`). `show` lists such keys under "Not part of the approval". `plan_revert` puts its conflicts, notes and warnings into the review block, so they are hashed and shown. The panel renders the review next to the actions when it can show it unchanged (see "Plan review in the panel"); it refuses Approve when output redaction, a size cap or a legacy format would make what it shows differ from what the hash covers. The command-line tool prints the plan and its hash, and the panel sends back the `plan_hash` of the list it rendered. The approval is refused if the plan on disk no longer has that hash when the person confirms, or if it no longer matches the hash stored when it was drafted. On approval the hash is stored as `approved_hash`.
- **An approved plan that is edited is refused.** Before an approved action runs (direct call or `execute_plan`), the server recomputes the hash and refuses if it differs from `approved_hash`.
- **A file a planned tool reads is bound by its content.** `revit_batch_create_sheets_from_csv` reads its CSV when the plan runs, so the path alone would let the file change after approval. For a tool listed in `CONTENT_BOUND_FILES` (`security/file_binding.py`, tool name to path argument), `plan_actions` reads the file through the workspace check and the size cap (1,000,000 bytes for the CSV) and writes its sha256 (`csv_sha256`) and row count (`csv_row_count`) into the action arguments, which the plan hash covers. A caller-supplied digest that differs is refused, and a file that is missing, outside the workspace or not a valid sheet CSV is refused at drafting. The plan listing shows `bound_files` (path, sha256, rows) and a line in `preview_markdown`. `execute_plan` checks every open bound action up front, a claim checks its action before consuming it, and the payload builder parses the same bytes it checked, so nothing is sent to Revit when the content differs: "the CSV changed after the plan was approved; draft a new plan" A missing file is refused the same way. A plan drafted before this change has no digest and is refused; draft it again. Other file-reading write tools opt in by adding an entry.
- **The approval record is signed.** Every approval, from the panel or `aec-model-bridge-approve`, goes through `ApprovalGate.update_plan_state`, which stores `approval_sig`: an HMAC-SHA256 over a canonical JSON encoding of `plan_id`, `approved_hash`, the approval state, `approved_via`, `approved_by`, `approved_at` and the plan's `binding` when it has one (`security/approval_signing.py`). The key is 32 random bytes made once per workspace on the first approval, at `plans/.keys/approval-signing.key`, inside the folder the workspace sandbox reserves from tools. It is created with mode 0600 and never overwritten. On POSIX a key file that is a symlink, owned by another user or readable by group or others is refused. On Windows file modes do not apply; the key relies on the workspace being in the user's profile (the default is `~/Documents/AEC Model Bridge`), which other standard users cannot read (UNVERIFIED on a live Windows install). The key is never logged and no tool returns it. `execute_plan`, a direct call that carries a `plan_id`, `rollback_plan` and `run_pyrevit_script` refuse a plan whose signature is missing or does not verify with "This plan's approval record does not verify; approve it again." This includes plans approved before the upgrade (fail closed): approve them again. Deleting the key file rotates it; every approved plan that has not run must then be approved again.
- **Each approved action runs at most once.** A tool call that carries a `plan_id` must match a not-yet-run action in that plan (same tool, same arguments; `plan_id`, `run_async` and `idempotency_key` are ignored). The action is consumed before the tool runs, under a per-plan lock and with a per-action claim file created exclusively (`plans/.claims/`). Concurrent calls for the same action therefore run it once, and editing an action's state back to `pending` does not reopen it. A provider-reported failure keeps the action consumed and marks it `failed`, making the plan `partial`; ask for a new plan to retry. A soft wait that returns `running` stays in flight until Revit reports a final result; a lost connection or expired request id leaves it `running` for human recovery. A `run_async` call consumes its action when it is queued.
- **Still running is not done.** A tool that answers `{"status": "running", "request_id": ...}` (the add-in kept working past the soft wait) leaves its action `running` with the claim consumed. `ApprovalGate.mark_in_flight` writes `plans/.inflight/<request_id>.json` (plan id, action id, tool), so a restarted server still knows. When `revit_get_result` (or `revit_job_status` for a `revit_run_job` job, keyed `job_<id>`) returns a final result, `settle_in_flight` closes the action: `executed` on success, `failed` with Revit's message on failure. Only Revit's own verdict closes it; a lost connection or an expired id leaves it `running` for the human `recover` command. A late result never reopens or overwrites an action that is already closed or abandoned.
- **A person can withdraw an approval.** A plan that is `approved` but not yet fully executed can still be rejected (panel or `aec-model-bridge-approve reject`). Executed or rolled-back plans cannot be rejected.
- **The command-line tool prints model text safely.** Control and format characters in tool names, argument keys and values (terminal escape sequences, carriage returns, bidirectional overrides) are shown as visible escapes such as `\x1b`. A plan whose arguments are not an object is shown with a plain message and cannot be approved.
- **Approval modes.** `MCP_REVIT_APPROVAL_MODE` takes one of three modes (the value is trimmed and case-insensitive):
  - `look_only`: every tool that changes the model is refused with "Look only mode: this tool changes the model. Switch to Ask me first in the panel or settings." Tools that only read keep working. The refusal applies on every path a model can reach (MCP calls, the panel's chat assistant, recipe steps and other module tool executors, `execute_plan`, and the panel's `/execute` route), and `rollback_plan` is refused too. A plan can still be drafted, but nothing in it can run until the mode is changed.
  - `ask_first` (the default; `required` is the older name and means the same): a mutating tool needs an approved, unchanged plan action, as described above.
  - `auto`: unplanned writes are permitted (see "Not protected"). The panel can also select timed Auto or explicit Dev; neither relaxes a configured Look only baseline. Dev retains strict checks for any supplied plan id.
- **`approval_mode` fails closed.** Any value that is not one of `look_only`, `ask_first`, `required` or `auto` (a typo, an empty string, `off`, `false`) behaves as `ask_first` and logs a warning. Earlier wording of this rule said `required`; it is the same behaviour under the new name.
- **The mode cannot be changed over MCP.** No MCP tool sets it. The starting mode comes from the environment variable (or the server configuration). The timed live change is the panel's **Auto for a limited time** switch (Settings > Approval mode): after a confirmation it posts to the hub's `POST /approval-mode` route (per-user token required, like every hub route), which writes `.approval-mode.json` in the workspace for 15 minutes to 8 hours (default 30). The record is signed with HMAC-SHA256 keyed by the hub token, which lives outside the workspace, so a file an agent writes into the workspace is ignored. Every gate that shares the workspace (the agent's MCP server, the hub, the CLI) honours it on its next call, and it ends by itself; a missing, expired, unsigned or malformed record means the process's starting mode applies. It only moves `ask_first` to `auto`: a `look_only` start is never relaxed. Like the token, this proves a local process running as you, not that a person clicked. The hub reports the mode in force, normalised to `look_only`, `ask_first` or `auto`, plus `auto_expires_at`, in `/diagnostics`, and the panel shows a countdown chip. Not yet verified against a live Revit session; covered by `tests/test_approval_override.py`.

### Explicit development mode

Settings also offers **Dev: stays on until switched off**, separately from timed Auto. After confirmation, the authenticated hub writes an HMAC-signed `.dev-mode.json` workspace record that must match an owner-only nonce authority beside the panel token. Switching Dev off revokes that authority before clearing the workspace record, so restoring an old signed record cannot re-enable it. Invalid, unsigned, revoked or unreadable records are ignored. Every process sharing the workspace observes it; it survives restarts and has no expiry or document binding. No MCP tool enables Dev. Selecting Ask first clears both live overrides; selecting timed Auto replaces Dev with the expiring window. The configured baseline still applies after an override is cleared.

Dev permits unplanned writes while retaining Look only lockdown. Calls supplying a plan id still require an unchanged, unused approved action. Diagnostics and `revit_get_context` identify Dev with `dev_mode: true`, effective `approval_mode: "auto"` and no Auto expiry; the panel displays Dev explicitly. Mode switches and Dev calls are audited, and an audit-write failure refuses the call. A mutating call uses one authorization snapshot for mode, audit and supplied-plan enforcement, so a concurrent switch cannot allow an unaudited write or bypass the plan checks. Workspace path checks, secret/path redaction, panel authentication and Python read-mode guards stay enforced. Optional folder/path relaxations are not implemented. See [ADR 0018](adr/0018-explicit-development-mode.md). The installed Revit 2024 backend reported Dev active during read-only smoke checks; mutating scratch-model acceptance remains pending.

### Which tools the gate covers (fail closed)

- **Proxied tools.** Tools forwarded to an external MCP server (`providers/proxy.py`) are unknown to this server, so each one is treated as a model change and needs an approved plan. It skips the gate only if its upstream name starts with `get_`, `list_`, `read_`, `query_`, `search_` or `describe_` and the upstream advertises `readOnlyHint: true`. If the upstream sends no `readOnlyHint` at all, the name prefix alone decides. `readOnlyHint: false` or `destructiveHint: true` always means gated. Users of proxied servers therefore need plan approval for any proxied write.
- **Navisworks.** Only `health`, `get_document_info`, `get_model_tree`, `get_selection`, `list_viewpoints`, `list_clash_tests` and `get_clash_results` skip the gate. Every other Navisworks tool, including any added later, is gated. This includes `navisworks_reflect_get` and `revit_reflect_get`: a property getter on an arbitrary object can have side effects.
- **UNVERIFIED:** `revit_calculate_material_quantities` stays ungated although the Revit add-in marks it mutating. The flag looks wrong, but this needs a Revit run to confirm; it is listed in `KNOWN_UNGATED` in `tests/test_addin_hub_contract.py`.

### Workspace policy

An optional `policy.yaml` (or `MCP_REVIT_POLICY_FILE`) can block tools or parameters, limit categories and cap plan size. It is checked when a plan is drafted and again just before `execute_plan` runs its first action, so a tightened policy stops plans that were drafted earlier. It only adds refusals: approval stays with a person, and no policy rule approves or runs a plan. The optional `require_second_approver` rule (off by default) records `requested_by` on the plan, inside the hash, and refuses an approval by that same name; an unknown requester or approver is refused. Both names come from the environment of the server and of the approving process (`MCP_REVIT_REQUESTER`, `MCP_REVIT_APPROVER`), never from tool arguments, and they are not verified identities. Names are compared ignoring case and any domain part, so `alice`, `alice@corp` and `CORP\alice` are the same person. The two-person rule records names and catches mistakes and same-account approval. It is not an authentication control: the approver name comes from `MCP_REVIT_APPROVER` or the operating-system account and is not verified, so one person with a shell can set another name. A separate approver needs a separate operating-system account or a separately configured approving machine. The rule is checked again when the plan runs: a plan with no recorded requester, or approved by its requester, does not execute while the option is on. An invalid file refuses all plan drafting and execution. See [Policy file](configuration-reference.md#policy-file).

### Machine policy and tiers

An administrator can set a machine policy file: `MCP_REVIT_MACHINE_POLICY_FILE`, else `%PROGRAMDATA%\AECModelBridge\policy.yaml` on Windows or `/etc/aec-model-bridge/policy.yaml` elsewhere. No file at the default location means no machine policy. A file named by `MCP_REVIT_MACHINE_POLICY_FILE` that is missing, and any file that cannot be read or is invalid, refuses every write. It uses the same keys as the workspace policy, and the stricter rule wins: blocked lists are joined, allowed lists are intersected, number limits take the smaller value, and a tier that is off in either file is off. A workspace policy can only tighten the machine policy.

Every tool has one tier. `script`: runs code or reaches arbitrary API members (`revit_execute_python`, invoke and reflect tools, `revit_run_job`, and `revit_raw_command`, which can forward any add-in command). `write`: changes the model, plus `plan_actions`, `execute_plan` and `plan_revert`. `export`: writes files or state outside the model. `read`: everything else. Set `allowed_tiers` or `blocked_tiers` to turn a tier off. Its tools are hidden from `tools/list`, calls are refused with a message naming the policy file by level and file name (through MCP, the panel, the chat assistant and module tools alike), and plan actions that use them are refused. Approve, reject, roll back, list plans, policy show, proof bundle and job status or cancel tools are never hidden or refused, so a person can always reject a plan.

Explicit Dev mode lifts the limits of both files. The AI cannot switch it on. Each bypassed call or plan is written to `dev-mode-audit.jsonl` with the rule it bypassed. Writes still go through `plan_actions`, approval and `execute_plan`. Dev mode does not lift an unreadable or invalid policy file. The server sends no `tools/list_changed`, so a client lists tools again after Dev mode or a policy file changes. `aec-model-bridge-doctor` shows the policy files, their hashes, the tiers that are off and whether the Dev override is active.

UNVERIFIED: the Windows ProgramData path and the ACL that keeps standard users from editing the file were not checked on a live Windows machine. Set the ACL so only administrators can write it. A path set with the environment variable is only as safe as the place that sets it.

### Plan review in the panel

The panel's `/execute` route adds a `review_view` to each plan in a `list_pending_plans` result and drops the raw `review` key from that copy. The hub computes it: `status` is `none` (a hash_version 1 plan with nothing outside its hash), `ok` (a hash_version 2 plan whose review is canonical, whose `reverts_plan_id` has the shape `plan_` plus 12 hex digits, and whose stored hash matches its content) or `invalid`. It also carries `hash_version`, `reverts_plan_id` and the normalised `review`. Through MCP and the chat, `list_pending_plans` is unchanged (no `review_view`); approve, reject and rollback stay human-only.

The hub sends `invalid`, and the panel disables Approve, when any of these holds:

- the review is missing, malformed, not canonical, or the plan does not match its stored hash;
- a legacy hash_version 1 plan has a `reverts_plan_id` or other content outside the hash (older revert plans keep their conflicts and warnings there), because the card cannot show it as approved content;
- a number in the actions or review is larger than 2^53-1 (a JavaScript page would show it rounded);
- **a credential would be masked.** The hub redacts every response, but the content a person approves is treated differently on the panel's `list_pending_plans` route: the actions (tool, arguments, before values), the review, the reverted plan id and any legacy revert metadata get only a narrow pass (`redact_for_approval`) that masks real credentials: the panel token, `Authorization` / `Bearer` values, `password:` / `api_key:` / `access_token:` / `client_secret:` text, values under exact secret key names (`api_key`, `password`, `secret`, `authorization`, `access_token`, `client_secret`, ...), key-shaped strings (`sk-...`, `ghp_...`, JWTs) and long high-entropy tokens. Paths, `code` arguments (the Python a `rhino_run_python` action would run), parameter names such as `Assembly Code`, and prose such as `Token: 3` or `Design session: 3 Oct` are shown as they are, because they are exactly what the person approves. If the narrow pass would mask anything, the plan is sent as `invalid` and Approve is disabled; the command-line tool does not redact, so `aec-model-bridge-approve show <plan id>` is the way to read and approve it. Everything outside the approved content, and every other route (logs, audit, diagnostics, MCP and chat results, proof bundles), keeps the full redaction (`redact_data`: paths, secret keys, `token:` text).

The Plans view shows the summary, reasoning, citations (rule id, clause, source), assumptions, excluded elements with reasons, warnings and conflicts. Each card states what the approval hash covers (the actions, the whole review and the reverted plan id) and lists what is covered but not shown (creation time, snapshot id, skipped list; `show` prints them). The review is built only when the person clicks "Show the review", and Approve for a hash_version 2 plan stays off until they have. All review text is untrusted: `textContent` only, control, bidi, Hangul-filler and braille-blank characters shown as escapes, runs of more than two combining marks cut, no links, unknown keys ignored, long fields clipped with "Show more (N more characters)". A list of more than 100 entries, or more than 50 pending plans, is not rendered in full: such a review blocks Approve (use the command-line tool) and extra plans are announced as not shown. Every card shows the plan id and the command `aec-model-bridge-approve show <plan id>` with a Copy button (clipboard use in WebView2 is UNVERIFIED; the command is selectable text). The action text is shown up to 4,000 characters with "Show all actions (N more characters)". The hub sorts pending plans newest first and sends at most 50 with an `omitted` count, so a flood of drafts cannot hide the plan just proposed; the panel announces the omitted count. Plans holding NaN or Infinity are refused at drafting, and a plan file that holds one is sent as a stub marked `invalid`, so it cannot break the whole queue.

**Fail closed.** If the review cannot be shown completely or at all (any `invalid` case above, a malformed view, a list over the cap, or an exception while drawing), Approve is disabled, also in Approve Selected, the card says to use `aec-model-bridge-approve show <plan id>`, and the page refuses to send `plan.approve` for it. UNVERIFIED: behaviour in the live WebView2 panel in Revit; the tests run the real page in headless Chromium with a stubbed host.

### Before any release: panel token and routing

Known gaps in the panel hub token and routing work, not fixed yet:

- **Plans must record the Revit that created them.** Store the originating pid, process start time and Revit version inside the hashed plan, and refuse `execute_plan`, `rollback_plan` and revert on a different instance (and refuse an unrouted plan when more than one Revit is live). Until then a plan drafted in Revit A can run against Revit B. Waiting on the proof-bundle change to land first.
- **The client sends the raw token to whatever listens on 127.0.0.1:8787.** On a shared machine another user could bind the port first. Use a challenge-response (the client sends an HMAC of a nonce and the path, and checks an HMAC from the hub) or check the socket owner before sending.
- **Hub thread cap.** The hub runs at most `AEC_PANEL_MAX_THREADS` request threads (default 32, range 4-256). Two of them serve only requests whose path is `/execute`; the tool name is in the body, so the reservation covers every `/execute` call, not only approve and reject. When every slot is in use, a new connection is answered 503 with `Retry-After: 1` and `{"ok": false, "kind": "hub_busy", ...}` before any thread starts. Each connection also has a 30 s socket timeout, so slow clients can hold a slot for up to 30 s per blocking read; enough of them can still delay the panel. `/execute` and `/agent/chat` have per-route rate limits for authenticated requests ([Configuration reference](configuration-reference.md#timeouts-and-rate-limits)). Tested with local sockets; UNVERIFIED with the live panel in Revit.
- **Routed-bridge cache hygiene:** the routed-bridge lock is held during a network initialise, and cached clients for dead Revits are not evicted.
- **Build and multi-instance acceptance.** The Revit 2024 add-in was built, installed and exercised with bounded read-only checks. Other target-runtime builds and two simultaneous live Revits still need acceptance; the single-instance smoke checks do not establish multi-instance routing.

### Not protected

- **`MCP_REVIT_APPROVAL_MODE=auto`** and the panel's timed Auto window permit unplanned writes. A call that supplies a `plan_id` skips the approval checks in these modes, but it still uses the claim files in `plans/.claims/`: a matching action is claimed before it runs, and a call whose matching actions were all claimed before is refused, even if their state was reset on disk. An action runs at most once in every mode. Explicit Dev also permits unplanned writes, but a supplied plan id must pass approval, hash and single-use checks. Human-only tools remain refused on AI tool-call paths in every mode. Use `look_only` instead when you want the opposite: no model changes at all.
- **The panel's `/execute` endpoint authenticates a local process, not a person.** It needs the per-user token (see the panel hub token section above) and passes the Host, Origin and Content-Type checks, which keeps out browser pages and other Windows users. Any process running as you can read the token file and approve a plan through it (recorded as `panel`). The panel's Plans view shows, for each pending plan, the escaped tool and arguments, and a before-value only when one was captured. `plan_actions` captures a before-value only for `revit_set_parameter_value`; for every other action (deletes, batch updates and so on) the before-state is recorded empty and the panel shows no before row, so a missing row does not mean nothing changes. `aec-model-bridge-approve show` remains the independent cross-check. The Plans view lists pending plans only (`ApprovalGate.list_pending_plans`); `aec-model-bridge-approve show <plan_id>` works for a plan in any state, while `proofs/` bundles exist only for plans that were executed (or attempted); approved-but-unexecuted and rejected plans have none.
- **The command-line tool does not authenticate who is typing.** Software that can run shell commands as you can run `aec-model-bridge-approve approve <id> --yes`. Do not give an AI client a shell on the same account if you rely on the gate.
- **Names are not identities.** `approved_by` is the local account name, not a verified person.
- **Write access to the workspace weakens the hash check.** The hashes detect a plan that was changed after drafting or approval, and the signature detects an approval record that was written or edited without the key. Software that can read the plans folder can read the key and sign its own records, and software that can write it can delete claim files. Keep AI clients' file tools out of the workspace folder.
- Plans drafted before this change have no `plan_hash` and cannot be approved; draft them again.

### Before any release: approval gaps

- **Panel approval and redaction.** The panel shows approved content unredacted except for real credentials (see "Plan review in the panel"). A plan that contains a password, key, bearer value or high-entropy token is shown with Approve disabled and must be approved with `aec-model-bridge-approve`. Consequence to accept or revisit: because paths and `code` arguments are now sent to the add-in host in clear, anything that can read the hub response (it needs the per-user panel token) sees them; they are the same text `show` prints. The credential detector is heuristic: a secret that does not look like one of the patterns above is shown as typed. UNVERIFIED in a live Revit panel.
- **Stuck `running` actions (recoverable by a person).** An action is claimed (O_EXCL marker) before it runs. If the process dies mid-call it stays `running`, and the plan cannot finish. Nothing recovers it automatically, because the call may have partly applied. `aec-model-bridge-approve show <plan_id>` lists each running action with its age (`STALE` after 15 minutes). `aec-model-bridge-approve recover <plan_id> --reason "..."` marks it `abandoned` (reason, time and local account recorded) and moves an approved plan to `partial`. An abandoned action is never run again and the plan's remaining actions cannot run either; draft and approve a new plan for them. Actions younger than 15 minutes need `--force`. There is no tool, MCP or panel route for this; check in Revit what the action changed before you plan again.
- **File replace on Windows.** Plan, claim and index writes use `os.replace`, which can fail with `PermissionError` while antivirus or a panel poll holds the file. The shared writer in `security/approval.py` retries up to 5 times with a 10-50 ms backoff, then raises a clear error and leaves the old file untouched. Not yet observed on Windows (UNVERIFIED). `security/proof.py` has its own `os.replace` that does not use the helper yet.
- **Approvals expire and are bound to a document ([ADR 0017](adr/0017-approval-document-binding-and-expiry.md)).** An approved plan is usable for `approval_ttl` (default 8 hours, `MCP_REVIT_APPROVAL_TTL`, `0` = no limit). The age is checked when a call runs; an older approval blocks new action claims and a person must approve a newly drafted plan for unstarted work. Already claimed actions can finish or be recovered and retain their proof. A fully successful plan finishes as `executed`; a plan with failed or unstarted actions finishes as `partial`. A plan with no started actions remains `expired`. Drafts expire too: a pending plan older than `pending_ttl` (default 14 days) cannot be approved and is hidden from `list` and `list_pending_plans` (reported as `expired_hidden`; `list --all` or `include_expired` shows it). Expired plans are never deleted, and neither check can be changed by a tool argument. A timestamp that is missing or lies in the future counts as expired. When a plan is drafted with a live Revit, a `binding` (document guid, hash of the central path, title, Revit version, and the active view id when an action names a `view_id`) is stored inside the hashed plan (a plan without the key hashes exactly as before). Executing it in another document is refused with both names; so is a bound plan whose live document cannot be read (Revit busy or closed). With no live Revit (mock mode, Revit busy at drafting, a document with no guid or central path) the binding is recorded as `null` and the plan is **not** refused for the document; `show` says "NOT BOUND". When `revit_get_context` reports `revit.pid` and `revit.started_at`, the binding records both, and a plan is refused in another Revit process, or after a restart, even with the same file open (a plan without them is document-bound only). `execute_plan` reads the live document once and reuses it for 10 seconds, so a 20-action plan makes one probe. The proof bundle and the panel redaction guard include the binding. A refusal before the first action leaves the plan `approved`. The check runs when an action is claimed and up front in `execute_plan`; the legacy `rollback_plan` does not use it. The panel list API carries `binding` and `expired`; the panel page does not display them yet (`show` does). UNVERIFIED against a live Revit, in particular workshared, detached and linked models.
- **Known limit (large plans):** each claimed action rewrites the whole plan file and re-verifies it, so executing a plan costs O(n^2) in its action count; keep plans to a few hundred actions.
- **Release note:** reject any pending revert plan drafted before upgrading. Older revert plans keep their conflicts, notes and warnings outside the hash; `show` prints them under "NOT covered by the approval".

---

## 5. Audit logging and sensitive data redaction

The audit recorder writes one line per tool call to an append-only file. See [Logging and audit](logging-and-audit.md) for what each log covers and for a caveat about which server writes the file.

### Log configuration
- Set the file with `MCP_REVIT_AUDIT_LOG`. The default is `audit.log` in the working directory of the server process.
- Set the level with `MCP_REVIT_LOG_LEVEL`. The default is `INFO`.

### Redaction rules
Audit entries and tool responses pass through a redaction step. It keeps tokens, OAuth codes and local directories out of log files and out of the AI's context:
- **Sensitive keys**: fields such as password, token, api_key, authorization, secret, client_secret and auth codes become `<redacted>`.
- **System paths**: Windows, UNC and POSIX file paths become `<redacted-path>`.

Example log entry:
```json
{
  "timestamp": "2026-07-08T18:02:10.123456Z",
  "tool": "revit.export_schedule",
  "request_id": "req_abc123",
  "payload": {
    "document_path": "<redacted-path>",
    "schedule_name": "Door Schedule",
    "output_dir": "<redacted-path>"
  },
  "response": {
    "success": true,
    "output_path": "<redacted-path>"
  }
}
```

---

## 6. Threat model and safety checklist

### What the design guards against
- Path traversal that tries to read sensitive files or settings.
- Unauthorized cloud calls. Credentials stay outside the tool arguments, in environment variables or keyrings.
- Malformed input that could crash Revit. The process boundary and input schemas prevent it.

### What is out of scope (host machine security)
- Other software on the same machine that can reach the loopback port. The opt-in named pipe ([ADR 0021](adr/0021-named-pipe-transport.md)) limits the pipe to the current Windows user; the HTTP port stays open beside it.
- Physical access to the machine, and malware running as your user.
- Bugs in vendor APIs (Autodesk Revit, Rhino).

### Safety checklist
- [ ] Set `MCP_REVIT_WORKSPACE_DIR` to a dedicated folder.
- [ ] Limit `MCP_REVIT_ALLOWED_DIRECTORIES` to the folders you need.
- [ ] Confirm no bridge listens on `0.0.0.0` or sits behind a port forward.
- [ ] Restrict access to the audit log file (`audit.log` by default).
- [ ] Keep `MCP_REVIT_APPROVAL_MODE` at `ask_first` (or `required`), so every model change needs an approved plan. Use `look_only` to block model changes entirely.

=== FILE: docs/proof-and-revert.md ===

# Proof bundles and revert plans

Status: in 1.5.0. Write-back and revert are not yet checked in a live Revit (UNVERIFIED; see below).

Every plan that finishes executing leaves a proof file, and an executed parameter fix can be undone through the same approval gate.

## Proof bundle

When `execute_plan` finishes (or a mutating tool marks a plan executed), the server writes `proofs/<plan_id>.json` in the workspace. Read it with the read-only tool `get_proof_bundle(plan_id)`.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `plan_id`, `tool`, `tools` | The plan and the tool(s) it called. |
| `created_at`, `approved_at`, `executed_at` | Lifecycle timestamps (UTC). |
| `approved_by` | The operating-system account that ran the approval (set by the server; an `approver` argument is ignored). It is a local account name, not a verified person. `approver_note` names the channel (`panel` or `cli`), or says the identity was not recorded. |
| `document` | `snapshot_id`, `doc_guid`, `doc_title` of the snapshot the plan was drafted from. `null` if the plan has no `snapshot_id`. |
| `plan_hash` | SHA-256 of the plan content (actions, arguments, before values, skipped list). |
| `elements` | Applied changes: `element_id`, `uid` (when a snapshot is known), `parameter`, `before`, `before_storage_type` (Revit storage type reported when `before` was captured; `null` if unknown), `new`. |
| `skipped` | Elements left out, each with a `reason` (blocked at planning time, or failed at execution). Entries from `parameter_manager_plan_set_params` carry `uid`, `element_id` and `param`. |
| `outcome` | `success`, `partial` or `failed`. Only `success` means every action ran. |

To get the document identity and the skipped list, pass `snapshot_id` (and `skipped`, which `parameter_manager_plan_set_params` returns as its blocked list) to `plan_actions`.

## Reverting

`plan_revert(plan_id)` reads the proof bundle and drafts a new pending plan that sets each parameter back to its recorded `before` value. It never executes anything: the draft still needs a person to approve it (in the panel or with `aec-model-bridge-approve`) and then `execute_plan`, and its own execution gets its own proof (`reverts_plan_id` links them).

It refuses, with a message, when:

- the plan has no proof bundle, or its outcome is not `success` (partial and failed runs are not reverted);
- the plan state is not `executed`;
- an element has no recorded `before` value (an empty value counts as not recorded);
- the current model value differs from the value the plan wrote. With `allow_conflicts=true` the draft is created anyway and lists those elements in the plan's hashed `review` block (`review.conflicts`, with element, parameter, expected, actual and revert-to values clipped for display, plus a warning; conflicts beyond the detailed list are named in an "Also changed" warning), so editing them after drafting invalidates the approval. `aec-model-bridge-approve show` and the panel review card display them.

Values are compared and drafted by type. The live read returns every value as text, so the staleness check compares numerically when both sides are numbers (`"60"` equals `60`, `"61"` does not) and as text otherwise. The drafted `value` is rebuilt from `before_storage_type`: integer for Integer and ElementId, float for Double, text for String. When the storage type was not recorded (proofs written before this field existed), a numeric-looking `before` becomes a number only if the value the plan wrote was numeric; the draft's `review.assumptions` list each such guess. The proof bundle also records the plan's `hash_version` and `review`.

Like `plan_actions`, drafting a revert is not itself gated; changing the model is.

## Limitations

- UNVERIFIED: write-back to Revit. The tests use an in-memory fake parameter store. The `outcome` reflects what the provider reported; the server does not re-read values after writing. Confirm against a live Revit session before relying on it.
- UNVERIFIED: revert's staleness check and the `before` capture read values through `revit_get_parameter_value`, so their correctness in a real model (units, type vs instance parameters, worksharing ownership) depends on that live tool.
- When a mutating tool is called directly with a `plan_id` (not through `execute_plan`), no per-action results exist. The proof is still written, but its outcome is never `success`, so such plans cannot be reverted. Direct calls that raise before the plan is marked executed leave no proof.
- Only `revit_set_parameter_value` actions are recorded per element and reverted. Other actions in the same plan appear under `other_actions` and are not reverted.
- `approved_by` is the local operating-system account name; it is not an authenticated identity.

=== FILE: docs/logging-and-audit.md ===

# Logging and audit

The project keeps two separate logs:

- the Python-side audit log
- the Revit add-in runtime log

## Python audit log

The code is in [packages/mcp-server-revit/src/revit_mcp_server/security/audit.py](../packages/mcp-server-revit/src/revit_mcp_server/security/audit.py).

`AuditRecorder.record()` writes one JSON line per tool call. Each line holds:

- a UTC timestamp
- the tool name
- the request ID
- the payload
- the response
- `prev_hash` and `hash`, a SHA-256 chain

Tokens, secrets and file paths are replaced before the line is written. See [Security](security.md). Set the file with `MCP_REVIT_AUDIT_LOG`. The default is `audit.log` in the working directory of the server process.

This log shows what the MCP server asked for.

### Tamper evidence

Each line holds the hash of the line before it (`prev_hash`) and a hash of its own content (`hash`). The first chained line uses 64 zeros as `prev_hash`. Lines are still plain JSON.

Check a log:

```bash
python -m revit_mcp_server.security.audit verify audit.log
```

The command prints a JSON result and exits 1 if the chain is broken. `verify_audit_log(path)` does the same in Python. Edited, reordered or removed middle lines are reported with the line number. Lines written before chaining existed are accepted only at the start of the file.

Limits: removing lines from the end of the file is not detected, and anyone who can rewrite the whole file can rebuild the chain. Keep a copy of the last hash somewhere else if you need to rule that out.

Note: in the current code, only the legacy server (`legacy/server.py`) creates an `AuditRecorder`. The main server (`mcp_server.py`) uses the same redaction but does not write this file. If `audit.log` is missing, this is the likely reason.

## MCP log messages

The server declares the MCP `logging` capability. A client sends `logging/setLevel` with `debug`, `info`, `notice`, `warning`, `error`, `critical`, `alert` or `emergency`, and the server sends each log message at or above that level as a `notifications/message`. A client that has not sent `logging/setLevel` receives no messages. The level is kept per client session. The code is in [packages/mcp-server-revit/src/revit_mcp_server/mcp_logging.py](../packages/mcp-server-revit/src/revit_mcp_server/mcp_logging.py).

- Messages come from the `revit_mcp_server` loggers. Log files and stderr are unchanged.
- Each message passes the same redaction as tool results: secrets and file paths always, personal data per `MCP_REVIT_REDACT_RESPONSES`.
- Only the message text is sent, cut to 2,000 characters. Tracebacks are never sent.
- A message that cannot be delivered is dropped.

## Add-in runtime log

The Revit add-in starts Serilog in [App.cs](../packages/revit-bridge-addin/src/Bridge/App.cs).

- The log file is `%APPDATA%\AECModelBridge\Logs\bridge.jsonl`.
- The log rolls over daily.
- It records add-in startup, shutdown, incoming requests and execution errors.

The panel hub writes its own log, `panel-hub.log`, in the same folder.

This log shows what Revit received and ran.

## Why there are two logs

The Python server and the Revit add-in run as separate processes. They do not share a runtime.

- The Python audit log tells you what the MCP server believed it asked for.
- The add-in log tells you what Revit actually received and ran.

When you investigate a problem, read both.

## What to expect when something fails

If the server sends a request and Revit fails to run it:

- The Python audit log may still look normal.
- The add-in log usually holds the useful error.

If the server rejects a path, or the payload has the wrong shape, the request never reaches the add-in:

- Look at the Python audit log and the error the client showed.
- The add-in log will have nothing for this request.

## Rule of thumb

Do not rely on one log alone. For a failed live request, compare these three records:

1. the Python audit entry
2. the add-in log entry
3. the error the client showed

This check quickly shows whether the problem is the input, the connection or Revit itself.

=== FILE: docs/privacy.md ===

# Privacy

> **DRAFT for owner sign-off.** The project owner must read and approve this page before it is published or linked from a marketplace listing. Last code check: 2026-11-05, against the upcoming 1.5 release source.

AEC Model Bridge is software that runs on your own computer. This page says what it does with your data, in plain words. It is about the software in this repository. It is not about the AI service you connect to it, which has its own privacy terms.

## Short version

- The project runs no servers and collects no data about you. It has no telemetry, no analytics and no crash reporting.
- Your Revit model is read by software on your computer. Whatever the assistant reads from your model is sent to the AI provider you connected, because that is how the assistant can answer. That provider's privacy policy applies to it.
- Logs, plans and proof files stay in folders on your computer. You can delete them.
- If you turn it on (`MCP_REVIT_USAGE_COUNTS=on`), the server counts how often each tool is called, in a small file in your workspace, to build the optional `learned` tool profile. The file holds tool names, counts and dates only. It never leaves your computer. `MCP_REVIT_USAGE_COUNTS=off` turns it off.

## What runs on your computer

- The MCP server (a Python program) that your AI client starts.
- The Revit add-in and its side panel.
- A local connection between the two, on your own machine (`127.0.0.1`). It does not accept connections from other computers.
- Optional: the VS Code extension. It only checks that the local bridge is running.

## What leaves your computer

| What | Where it goes | When |
|---|---|---|
| Tool results the assistant reads from your model (element names, parameter values, counts and so on), and what you type in chat | The AI provider behind the client you use (for example Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or a local model) | Whenever you use the assistant. The project does not control or see this. Check your provider's privacy policy and your plan's data settings. |
| Chat messages and tool results from the Revit panel's built-in chat | The selected provider: Anthropic's API with `MCP_REVIT_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or the installed `claude` or `codex` command-line client. Claude and Codex use their configured AI service/account; that provider's privacy terms apply. | Only when you use the built-in chat |
| Requests to Speckle (default `https://app.speckle.systems`, or your own server) | Speckle | Only if you use the Speckle tools and sign in |
| Requests to Autodesk Platform Services (`developer.api.autodesk.com`) | Autodesk | Only if you use the cloud tools with your own Autodesk credentials |
| Downloads of the software itself (for example `uvx` fetching the server from GitHub, or `pip` fetching packages from PyPI) | GitHub, PyPI | When you install or update. Those services see the download request as for any download. |

If you use only mock mode (sample data, no Revit), the model data is fake sample data. The assistant still sends what it reads to your AI provider.

## What the project does not do

We searched the code in this repository (the Python server, the Revit and Rhino add-ins, the VS Code extension and the install scripts) for analytics, telemetry, crash reporting, update checks and calls to a project-run server. We found none. The network paths above include the local bridge, optional provider chat, Speckle, Autodesk Platform Services and the extension's local health check. This is a code review at the date above, not a guarantee about future versions. If that ever changes, it will be opt-in and written here first.

File arguments handled by the workspace guard are limited to the folders you allow. Approved host-script tools such as `revit_execute_python` and `rhino_run_python` run with the host process's file and network permissions; their script bodies are not sandboxed by the workspace guard. Review scripts before approving them. See [security.md](security.md).

## Where your files and logs live (Windows)

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Workspace: approval plans (`plans`), proof bundles (`proofs`), model snapshots (`snapshots`) and files the tools write | `Documents\AEC Model Bridge` by default, or the folder in `MCP_REVIT_WORKSPACE_DIR` |
| Tool usage counts (tool names, calls per day, last-used day; no arguments, results, model data or user names) | `<workspace>\usage\tool-usage.json`. Used only by the `learned` tool profile. Turn off with `MCP_REVIT_USAGE_COUNTS=off`; show or delete with `aec-model-bridge-usage show` or `reset`. See [learned-profile.md](learned-profile.md). |
| Audit log of tool calls (if enabled) | The file in `MCP_REVIT_AUDIT_LOG`. Secrets, tokens and file paths are redacted before writing. See [logging-and-audit.md](logging-and-audit.md). |
| Add-in log and panel log | `%APPDATA%\AECModelBridge\Logs` (`bridge.jsonl`, `panel-hub.log`) |
| Bridge endpoint files (which port Revit uses) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AECModelBridge\registry` |
| Installed program files | `C:\ProgramData\AECModelBridge` |
| Backups of your AI client settings made by the installer | Next to the original file, named `.aec-backup-<date>` |

Plans and proof bundles can contain element names and parameter values from your project. Treat the workspace folder as project data.

## How to delete everything

1. Close Revit and your AI client.
2. Uninstall: Windows *Apps > Installed apps > AEC Model Bridge > Uninstall*.
3. Delete these folders if they still exist: `Documents\AEC Model Bridge` (or your own workspace folder), `%APPDATA%\AECModelBridge`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AECModelBridge`, `C:\ProgramData\AECModelBridge`.
4. Delete the audit log file you set in `MCP_REVIT_AUDIT_LOG`, if any.
5. Remove the `aec-model-bridge` entry from your AI client's MCP settings, and delete any `.aec-backup-*` files you do not need.

Data held by your AI provider, Speckle or Autodesk is deleted through those services, not from this computer.

## Questions

Open an issue at <https://github.com/Sam-AEC/aec-model-bridge/issues>. For security problems, see [SECURITY.md](../.github/SECURITY.md).

=== FILE: docs/adr/0001-multi-provider-architecture.md ===

# ADR 0001: Multi-Provider AEC Automation Architecture

## Status
Accepted

## Context
The AEC Model Bridge is being expanded from a Revit-only MCP bridge to a multi-platform AEC automation platform. To accommodate diverse software systems (e.g., Rhino, Tekla, Archicad, IfcOpenShell, Autodesk Forma, Speckle) while maintaining existing Revit tools and compatibility, we need a unified provider architecture.

## Decisions

### 1. Provider Discovery and Registry
- **Headless & In-Process Providers**: Registered directly in a Python `ProviderRegistry` class.
- **Local Desktop Adapters**: Discoverable dynamically via local loopback ports. Desktop adapters will bind to dynamic loopback ports and register their active endpoint, process ID, and a security bearer token with a local registry.
- **Cloud Providers**: Discovered and loaded dynamically based on environment configuration or user credentials.

### 2. Transport Types
- **Headless/Local Files**: In-process Python imports (e.g., `IfcOpenShell`) for zero overhead and deterministic executions.
- **Desktop SDKs**: Isolated process HTTP/JSON-RPC boundaries over loopback (e.g., Revit bridge). This isolates non-redistributable SDKs and prevents C# crashes from bringing down the MCP server.
- **Cloud Integrations**: Secure HTTPS REST/GraphQL protocols.
- **Batch/Compute Engines**: Asynchronous HTTP/WebSocket queues with job status polling.

### 3. Capability Manifests
Each provider publishes a runtime capability manifest:
```json
{
  "provider_id": "ifc",
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "ifc_get_metadata",
      "description": "Read file headers and schemas...",
      "input_schema": { ... },
      "output_schema": { ... },
      "is_mutating": false,
      "confirmation_required": false,
      "execution_mode": "sync"
    }
  ]
}
```
The MCP server aggregates these manifests dynamically rather than hardcoding tool names.

### 4. Object References
Instead of designing a universal BIM object model, we use a flexible reference envelope that preserves native identities:
```json
{
  "provider": "ifc",
  "project_id": null,
  "model_id": "structure.ifc",
  "object_id": "12345",
  "stable_id": null,
  "ifc_guid": "2XQ$n5SLP5MBLyL6JQj8Z0",
  "version": "v1"
}
```
Different platforms map object identities via standard fields like `ifc_guid` or external mapping tables.

### 5. Authentication and Security
- **Desktop/Local**: Every local desktop bridge generates a random per-session bearer token (nonce) during startup. The client must supply this token in authorization headers. Loops back only to `127.0.0.1`.
- **Cloud (OAuth)**: Credentials must never appear in tool parameters, results, or logs. Use OS-level secure credential stores or environment variables loaded into the server environment. OAuth code flow with PKCE is used for user-delegated access.

### 6. Mutation Controls
- Mutating tools support a `dry_run` parameter where applicable.
- Confirmations are requested before high-risk mutations.
- Transacted operations are wrapped in host transaction APIs (e.g., Revit transactions) to support undo.
- Idempotency keys are included for cloud operations.

### 7. Asynchronous Jobs
Long-running or batch operations yield a job reference:
```json
{
  "job_id": "job_9876",
  "status": "running",
  "progress_percent": 45,
  "artifacts": []
}
```
Clients poll or receive webhooks, with support for cancellation.

### 8. Licensing Boundaries
- Host SDK binaries (e.g., Autodesk Revit assemblies, RhinoCommon, Tekla Open API) must remain separate from the core repository.
- Code dependencies utilize standard interfaces. Connectors are packaged separately.
- Clear licensing boundaries apply (GPL/LGPL linking exemptions where required).

### 9. Compatibility and Legacy Support
- Existing `revit_*` tool names, routes, and `MCP_REVIT_` configuration are preserved.
- A Revit Compatibility Adapter maps legacy MCP calls directly to the new `RevitProvider`.
- Legacy configuration is mapped to provider configuration automatically.

## Consequences
- **Extensibility**: Adding a new AEC integration only requires writing a class that conforms to the `AECProvider` interface.
- **Robustness**: In-process libraries like `IfcOpenShell` do not require desktop software to run or test.
- **Isolation**: Prohibits licensing leakage and maintains strict desktop SDK process isolation.

=== FILE: docs/module-authoring.md ===

# Developer guide: module authoring

A module packages commands, workflows, schemas and QA rules. Developers and firms can add their own.

## 1. Directory structure

A module folder goes in one of these places:
- **Built-in**: `packages/mcp-server-revit/src/revit_mcp_server/modules/<module_id>/`
- **User or firm folder**: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AECModelBridge\modules\<module_id>\`. The server loads it only when `enable_user_modules` is `True`. Set this with the environment variable `MCP_REVIT_ENABLE_USER_MODULES`.
- **Installed package**: the package declares an `aec_model_bridge.modules` entry point.

```
<module_id>/
├── module.json      # Manifest (required)
├── module.py        # Python commands & hooks (optional)
├── rules/           # QA/QC YAML rule definitions (optional)
└── ui/              # HTML panel components (optional)
```

## 2. Manifest schema (`module.json`)

```json
{
  "id": "hello_world",
  "name": "Hello World Module",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "min_hub_version": "1.2.0",
  "description": "A demo module.",
  "author": "AEC Model Bridge",
  "license": "GPL-3.0-or-later",
  "requires_providers": ["revit"],
  "permissions": ["model.read"],
  "commands": [
    {
      "id": "say_hello",
      "title": "Say Hello",
      "surface": ["mcp"],
      "execution_mode": "sync",
      "is_mutating": false,
      "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "name": {"type": "string", "default": "World"}
        },
        "required": ["name"]
      }
    }
  ],
  "hooks": {
    "validate": "module:HelloWorldModule.validate",
    "on_result": "module:HelloWorldModule.on_result"
  }
}
```

## 3. Permissions

A manifest (and each command) may declare only these permission names. The list lives in `revit_mcp_server/security/module_permissions.py`; a test keeps this guide, the code and every built-in manifest in step.

- `model.read`: standard read tools.
- `model.write`: tools that change the model. The server always checks these against the action plan approval gate.
- `model.delete`: destructive operations.
- `params.write`: parameter value changes.
- `files.write`: writing files inside the sandboxed workspace.
- `net.local`: local connections.
- `net.cloud`: cloud sync.
- `python.host`: raw Python on the host, such as `revit_execute_python`. It stays off unless `allow_python_host` is `True`. Set this with `MCP_REVIT_ALLOW_PYTHON_HOST`.

An unknown name (a typo, or the old `workspace.write`, which is now `files.write`) logs a warning when the module loads. This is a warning for one release and will become a load error.

### What is enforced

- `python.host` is checked each time a command runs.
- `files.write`: the `workspace` argument a handler receives has `workspace.assert_writable(path)`. Call it on every path you are about to write. It does what `assert_in_workspace` does and also refuses with a `WorkspaceViolation` when neither the manifest nor the command declares `files.write`. `MCP_REVIT_MODULE_PERMISSION_MODE` is `enforce` (default) or `warn` (log and allow, for third-party modules that need time to declare the permission).
  Built-in modules use the same check: every built-in write path calls it, and a built-in whose manifest lacks `files.write` is refused. Modules run in the server process, so for a third-party module this covers handlers that use `assert_writable`; it is not a sandbox against code that calls `open()` directly.

## 3a. Importing other files from a module

The loader registers `module.py` in `sys.modules` as a plain module (`revit_mcp_server.modules.<id>`), not a package. A normal `from . import helper` or `import revit_mcp_server.modules.<id>.helper` fails, depending on load order. Load siblings by file path, for example with `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, Path(__file__).parent / "helper.py")` and `module_from_spec`, and do not import another module's code.

## 4. Hooks

- **`validate` hook**: runs before the command. Return `{"ok": true}` to continue. Return `{"blockers": ["Details"]}` to stop the command.
- **`on_result` hook**: runs after the command, asynchronously.

=== FILE: docs/rule-packs.md ===

# Shareable QA/QC rule packs

A rule pack is a YAML file of QA/QC rules. A firm can keep its naming,
numbering and standards checks in one file, share it, and run it with
`qaqc_checker_run_check`.

## Where packs live

- Built-in packs ship with the server (for example `core`).
- User packs live in `<workspace>/rule_packs/<name>.yaml`. The workspace is the
  first allowed directory of the server.

`run_check(rule_pack="<name>")` and `list_rules(rule_pack="<name>")` resolve a
pack name in this order: built-in first, then the workspace `rule_packs/`
folder. A user pack cannot shadow a built-in. Names may only contain letters,
digits, `_`, `-` and `.`; paths are not accepted, so a pack name can never point
outside those two folders. Packs are re-validated every time they are loaded.

## Tools

| Tool | Reads/writes | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `qaqc_checker_list_rule_packs` | read-only | Lists built-in and user packs with rule count and validity. |
| `qaqc_checker_validate_rule_pack` | read-only | Schema-checks a YAML file (`path`) or a named pack (`rule_pack`). Returns `errors` and `warnings`, each with `rule_id`, `field` and `message`. Never executes rules. |
| `qaqc_checker_import_rule_pack` | writes a file | Validates `source_path` (inside the workspace) and copies it to `rule_packs/<name>.yaml`. Refuses invalid packs, built-in names, and existing packs unless `overwrite=true`. |
| `qaqc_checker_export_rule_pack` | writes a file | Copies a built-in or user pack to `destination` (a file or folder inside the workspace; default `exports/<name>.yaml`). Refuses to overwrite unless `overwrite=true`. |

All paths are checked with the workspace path-safety helper (symlinks are
resolved), so nothing is read or written outside the workspace.

## Rule format

```yaml
rules:
  - id: door_mark_missing          # required, unique, letters/digits/_-.
    severity: error                # required: error | warning | info
    category: Doors                # optional label
    description: "Door has no Mark."   # required, becomes the issue message
    filter:                        # optional; see operators below
      category: OST_Doors
      parameter: {name: Mark, empty: true}
    assertion: "element_count == 0"    # optional, this is the default
    fix_template: "Set the Mark on '{label}'."   # optional, free text for a person
    fix: {parameter: Mark, value: "D-000"}       # optional, a concrete parameter write
```

`fix` names one parameter and one fixed value (text, number or true/false). Findings of a rule with a `fix` can be
selected by issue id in `qaqc_checker_draft_fix_plan`, which drafts one `plan_actions` list with a
`revit_set_parameter_value` action per finding. Findings of rules without a `fix` are listed as skipped.
The tool only drafts: a person approves the plan and `execute_plan` writes it. The validator rejects a pack with an invalid `fix`.

### Operators the engine supports

Filter keys (all must match):

- `category`: a category such as `OST_Doors`, or a list of them.
- `placed`: `true` or `false`.
- `parameter`: `{name: <Parameter>, empty: true}` or `{name: <Parameter>, value: "<text>"}`.
  `value` is an exact text comparison.
- `workset`: exact workset name.
- `family_source`: matches family types by source (for example `inplace`).
  Use it alone; combining it with element filter keys is rejected.

Assertions:

- `element_count == 0`: every element that matches the filter is an issue.
- `all elements have <field>`: matched elements missing that top-level element
  field are issues.

The validator rejects anything else, with the list of supported names in the
message. There is no regular-expression operator, so naming-pattern checks (for
example "door Mark must match `D-###`") cannot be expressed. Filter rules have
no uniqueness operator; a pipeline rule can find duplicate values with
`group_by` and `aggregate`, but its rows are groups, so those issues have no
element.

### Pipeline rules

A rule can use `pipeline` instead of `filter` and `assertion`. It holds
[snapshot_compute](snapshot-compute.md) steps, and every row of the last step
is an issue: `uid` gives the element, and `label` (if a step selects one),
`type_name` or `category` gives the label. Keep `uid` in the rows; a `select`
without it gives issues with no element. A row whose `uid` is not text (for
example a `list` aggregate named `uid`) fails the rule with an error.

```yaml
  - id: door_rating_below_wall
    severity: error
    description: "Door fire rating is lower than the fire rating of its host wall."
    pipeline:
      - join: [host]
        where:
          - {field: category, value: OST_Doors}
          - {field: params.Fire Rating, op: lt, value: {field: host.params.Fire Rating}}
```

- Pipelines can use joins, field-to-field comparisons, `spatial`, `group_by` and
  every other step key, so checks that `filter` cannot express fit in a pack.
- The validator checks the steps without a model and refuses unknown keys, ops,
  joins and aggregates with the step name. A rule with both `pipeline` and
  `filter` or `assertion` is refused.
- `link:` sources are refused in rule packs.
- Relation joins read the snapshot's relations in `run_check` and in the
  reports that run rule packs.
- A server older than this change warns that `pipeline` is an unknown field and
  runs the rule as if it had no filter, so every element becomes an issue. Use
  pipeline rules only with servers that support them.

[`docs/examples/rule_packs/door-room-pipeline.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/door-room-pipeline.yaml)
has the three `door-room-basics` rules written as pipelines, plus the rule
above. On the mock snapshot the three converted rules find the same issues as
the originals (`tests/test_qaqc_pipeline_rules.py`).

[`docs/examples/rule_packs/door-fire-rating.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/door-fire-rating.yaml)
reports doors rated lower than their host wall, doors without a rating, and doors
whose host wall has no rating. Ratings must be numbers in one unit. Set the parameter
name by replacing `Fire Rating` in the pack.

### Classification and COBie packs

Three example packs check asset categories for classification codes and COBie fields:

- [`classification-uniclass.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/classification-uniclass.yaml): Uniclass 2015 code (`Pr_20_93_52`).
- [`classification-omniclass.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/classification-omniclass.yaml): OmniClass number (`23-13 11 11`).
