- [`cobie-completeness.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/cobie-completeness.yaml): COBie component name and space, and type name, category and manufacturer.

Each field gets separate rules:

- `*_not_captured` (info): the element has no such parameter in the snapshot. The parameter does not exist on it, or the add-in did not read it. COBie type fields are read from the element's type.
- `*_missing`: the parameter is present but empty.
- `*_format` (classification packs only): the value has the wrong table prefix or separators.

Limits:

- The parameter names (`Uniclass Code`, `OmniClass Number`, `COBie Component Name` and so on) are assumptions. Replace them in the pack with your names. Pipeline paths split at dots, so a name such as `COBie.Component.Name` cannot be read; use a name without dots.
- The category list (doors, windows, mechanical, electrical and plumbing fixtures) is a starting point. Edit the `in` list in each rule.
- The format check looks at the table prefix and the separators only. The engine has no regex operator, so it does not check the digit groups. For the full pattern, save a reviewed naming rule with `target: parameter`.
- The packs are tested on fixture snapshots only. How the add-in captures these parameters in a live Revit model is UNVERIFIED.

### Model health packs

Four example packs check worksets, levels, shared parameters and view templates:

- [`workset-checks.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/workset-checks.yaml)
- [`level-checks.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/level-checks.yaml)
- [`shared-parameter-checks.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/shared-parameter-checks.yaml)
- [`view-template-checks.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/view-template-checks.yaml)

| Rule | Severity | Reports |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workset_not_captured` | info | No element in the snapshot has a workset (one issue, no element). |
| `workset_name_empty` | error | Empty workset name. |
| `workset_default_name` | warning | Element on `Workset1`. |
| `workset_name_padded` | warning | Workset name with a leading, trailing or double space. |
| `workset_levels_grids_not_shared` | warning | Level or grid not on `Shared Levels and Grids`. |
| `level_name_not_captured` | info | Level has no name in the snapshot. |
| `level_name_empty` | error | Empty level name. |
| `level_name_padded` | warning | Level name with a leading, trailing or double space. |
| `level_name_duplicate` | error | Two levels share a name (no element). |
| `level_elevation_not_captured` | info | Level has no `Elevation` parameter. |
| `level_elevation_duplicate` | error | Two levels share an exact elevation (no element). |
| `asset_id_not_captured`, `package_code_not_captured` | info | The parameter is not on the element. |
| `asset_id_empty` | error | `Asset ID` is empty. |
| `package_code_empty` | warning | `Package Code` is empty. |
| `view_template_not_captured` | info | View has no `View Template` parameter. |
| `view_template_unassigned` | warning | `View Template` is empty or `-1`. |

Not captured by the snapshot, so no rule:

- Shared parameter GUIDs. The snapshot keeps the name, value and storage type only. Checking a GUID needs an add-in change.
- The view template a view uses. The top-level `views` list has `is_template` but no assignment, and rules cannot read it. The view template pack reads a `View Template` parameter on view elements instead.
- The add-in snapshot does not write `workset` on elements. On a live snapshot only `workset_not_captured` fires.

Other limits:

- The `Asset ID` and `Package Code` names, the category list and the shared workset name are assumptions. Replace them in the pack.
- Duplicate rules group levels, so their issues have no element, and the issue store keeps one stored issue per rule for them. Run results list every duplicate.
- Level and view checks on a live model are UNVERIFIED. The packs are tested on fixture snapshots only (`tests/test_model_health_packs.py`).

Stored findings belong to their rule pack. Running one pack only reconciles that
pack's issues, and identical rule IDs in different packs stay independent.
Overwriting a pack refreshes its open issues' severity and message on the next run.
Existing databases migrate without deleting history; older issues without a pack
identity are assigned to `core`.

## Reviewed naming rules

A rule pack has no regular-expression operator. A naming rule is a separate, saved
kind of rule: a category, a regex the name must fully match, a message and a severity.
An agent can write one during a chat. It is kept only after a person approves it, and
it runs later with no model call.

| Tool | Reads/writes | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `qaqc_checker_test_naming_rule` | read-only | Runs a proposed rule against a snapshot. Returns the rule hash, `matches` and `misses`, each with a count and a sample (default 10, at most 25). Saves nothing. |
| `qaqc_checker_save_naming_rule` | mutating | Writes `<workspace>/naming_rules/<rule_id>.json`. It is gated like any write: `plan_actions`, a person approves the plan in the panel, then `execute_plan`. It is not a human-only tool, and it cannot run without an approved plan unless the person has switched approval off. Refuses an existing id unless `overwrite=true`. |
| `qaqc_checker_replay_naming_rules` | appends to a log | Runs every saved rule (or the ids in `rule_ids`) against a snapshot. No model call. The same snapshot gives the same findings, sorted by rule id and element uid. Returns `rule_hashes` and writes them to `<workspace>/naming_rules_audit.jsonl` with the snapshot id. |

`target` picks the value that is checked: `type_name` (default), `name`, `family`, or
`parameter` together with `parameter` (the parameter name). Elements are matched by
`category`. An empty value, or a value longer than 128 characters, is a miss and is not
passed to the regex.

The rule hash is the SHA-256 of the rule fields as sorted compact JSON. The rule file
stores it. Replay recomputes it and refuses a file that was edited, that has an invalid
regex, or whose id does not match its file name. Rule ids use the pack-name character
set and are built with the workspace path-safety helper, so a path never reaches the file
system.

### Which regexes are refused

Python's `re` has no timeout, so the check is made before the pattern runs. A regex is
refused when it:

- is empty, longer than 200 characters, or does not compile;
- uses a backreference or a lookaround;
- puts a variable repeat (`+`, `*`, `?`, `{m,n}`) inside another repeat, for example `(a+)+` or `(\w+\s?)+`;
- puts an alternation inside a repeat, for example `(a|aa)+`;
- has more than 3 unbounded repeats.

Safe patterns such as `[A-Z]{1,3}-\d{3}` or `(A|B)-\d+` pass. Together with the 128
character cap on names, the work per element stays small.

## Example pack

[`docs/examples/rule_packs/door-room-basics.yaml`](examples/rule_packs/door-room-basics.yaml)
covers door Mark, unplaced doors and room Number. To use it:

1. Copy the file into your workspace, for example `<workspace>/door-room-basics.yaml`.
2. `qaqc_checker_validate_rule_pack` with `path` set to that file.
3. `qaqc_checker_import_rule_pack` with `source_path` set to that file.
4. `qaqc_checker_run_check` with `rule_pack="door-room-basics"`.

To share your own pack, call `qaqc_checker_export_rule_pack` and send the
resulting YAML file; the recipient imports it the same way.

## IDS validation

`ids_validator_validate_ifc` checks an IFC file against a buildingSMART IDS file (`.ids` XML) with `ifctester` from IfcOpenShell. Both files must be inside the workspace. It needs the optional extra and refuses with an install hint without it:

```
pip install "aec-model-bridge[ids]"
```

The result gives pass, fail or skipped per specification (skipped means the specification is for another IFC schema version), the applicable, passed and failed entity counts, the failing GlobalIds with their class, name and reasons (at most `max_failed` per specification, default 50; the counts stay complete), and the requirement summary. `html_filename` and `json_filename` write a report inside the workspace. The IFC and IDS files are only read. This is separate from the rule packs above, which run on snapshots. `ifctester` is limited to 0.8.x because 0.9 needs a newer IfcOpenShell than this project locks.

=== FILE: docs/mcp-token-budget.md ===

# MCP token budget measurements

Measured 2026-11-05 with `MCP_REVIT_MODE=mock`, the supplied Python interpreter, a temporary workspace, no user modules or provider credentials, and no Revit model execution. Baseline captured at `87d1d1bb5312ccb9868786860cbc66f76c47b895` before production changes; results were reported before edits.

The checkout exposes **330** tools rather than the estimated 298. Sizes use SDK compact `ListToolsResult` / `CallToolResult` JSON (excluding JSON-RPC framing). Token estimates are characters / 4, not tokenizer counts or billed context. UTF-8 bytes, characters, inputs and per-tool data are retained in the JSON evidence files.

## Initial profile and response pass

*Dated: the 2026-11-05 measurements, before the 2026-11-16 metadata trims and compact reads; the follow-up sections below supersede these numbers.*

| Payload | Before characters | After characters | Before ~tokens | After ~tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Full catalogue (302 tools) | 358,133 | 330,418 | 89,533 | 82,605 |
| Daily catalogue (231 tools) | 358,133 | 255,533 | 89,533 | 63,883 |
| Metadata enrichment, full catalogue | 132,722 | 105,007 | 33,181 | 26,252 |
| Module listing, full compact | 55,697 | 38,465 | 13,924 | 9,616 |
| Module listing, full compact IDs | 55,697 | 4,216 | 13,924 | 1,054 |
| Module listing, daily compact | 55,697 | 33,157 | 13,924 | 8,289 |
| Module listing, daily compact IDs | 55,697 | 3,793 | 13,924 | 948 |
| revit_list_elements, compact | 350 | 301 | 88 | 75 |
| revit_list_families, compact | 305 | 267 | 76 | 67 |
| revit_get_element_parameters, compact | 352 | 303 | 88 | 76 |
| revit_list_views, compact | 373 | 284 | 93 | 71 |
| plan_actions, compact | 1,058 | 768 | 265 | 192 |

Full catalogue savings: **7.74%**. Daily catalogue savings versus baseline: **28.65%**, hiding 71 tools. Module IDs projection with full profile saves **92.43%** of that response. The full profile retains all original tools. The five default read responses and default plan response are unchanged; response savings above require explicit opt-in formatting. The existing shared initialization approval instructions remain present and unchanged (excluded from catalogue totals).

## Follow-up: metadata trims (2026-11-16)

Same method (mock mode, chars / 4 over `list_tools`), measured on this branch. Tool counts are unchanged (302 full, 231 daily).

| Step | Full ~tokens | Daily ~tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Before | 82,604 | 63,901 |
| Drop duplicate `annotations.title` (top-level `title` stays) | 80,114 | 61,970 |
| Short shared text for `dry_run`, `on_error`, `tag`, `limit`, `fields`, `status_labels`; `ids` item text dropped | 79,002 | 61,053 |
| One "Use X for A; use Y for B" sentence on 29 sibling tools | 79,688 | 61,740 |

Net: about 2,900 tokens fewer in full (3.5%) and 2,160 fewer in daily (3.4%). The sibling sentences add about 690 tokens on purpose, to help a model pick between near-duplicate tools. The shared parameter texts keep units, defaults and the rule that `dry_run` rolls back and writes nothing; only variants that said the same thing are replaced, tools with a different rule keep their own text. `plan_id` text and all approval wording are unchanged. The approval provider is now always visible, in every profile.

## Follow-up: compact reads, a size cap and paging (2026-11-16)

This changes what a read answer costs, not what the catalogue costs. The first pass above left default reads indented; that is no longer true for read-only tools.

- **Compact by default.** A tool with `readOnlyHint: true` returns minified JSON. `response_options.compact: false` brings back indented text. Tools that can write, and `plan_actions`, keep the old default (indented; compact only on request). Mock reads measured with the script below: `revit_list_elements` 260 to 221 characters, `revit_list_families` 221 to 191, `revit_get_element_parameters` 264 to 225, `revit_list_views` 276 to 200 (text content including the "executed successfully" line).
- **One size cap.** A read-only result over 20,000 characters (`DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS`) has its largest lists trimmed until it fits, stays valid JSON, and gets `truncated: true`, `total`, `returned`, `truncated_field` and a hint to narrow with limit/offset/count_only/fields or filters. `response_options.max_chars` sets another cap (0 = off). Short results, errors, running-job answers and every tool that is not read-only are never trimmed. In the mock catalogue `module_list_commands` (51,186 characters, full profile) now answers in 12,167; ask for `fields: ["modules.id", "modules.commands.id"]` or `max_chars: 0` to see more. `max_chars` is advertised on the five tools that already advertise `response_options`; any other read-only tool accepts `compact` and `max_chars` without listing them in its schema.
- **Never touched:** `plan_actions`, `execute_plan`, `list_pending_plans`, `get_proof_bundle`, `plan_revert`, the job tools and `revit_get_result`, and any result that carries `plan_id` or `plan_hash`. A test sends a 400-action plan (over 100,000 characters) through `call_tool` and checks the answer is byte-identical to the stored plan.
- **Paging.** `revit_list_elements`, `revit_list_views`, `revit_list_families`, `revit_get_categories`, `revit_get_warnings` and `revit_get_schedule_data` take optional `limit`, `offset` and `count_only`. The server slices the add-in's list after Revit answers (no add-in change), so Revit still builds the full list; only the answer is smaller. Without those arguments the result is unchanged except for the cap.

Catalogue cost of the new options (same method as above, mock mode): full 79,765 to 80,191 ~tokens (+0.5%), daily 61,799 to 62,225 (+0.7%); tool counts unchanged (302 and 231). The response savings above are separate from these totals and depend on what a live model returns.

## Follow-up: the `core` profile and a family map (2026-11-16)

Clients that load every tool pay for the whole catalogue on each session. Anthropic guidance says tool selection degrades past roughly 30-50 tools and that tool search pays off above about 10k tokens of definitions. `MCP_REVIT_TOOL_PROFILE=core` is a built-in profile that lists tools by name (not by provider or module ID) and keeps only the BIM-coordinator loop. The five approval tools stay visible in every profile, so core exposes 54 tools. Hidden tools are not listed and are refused at dispatch, in plan and job targets too, with a message that names `MCP_REVIT_TOOL_PROFILE=daily or full`.

Same method as above (mock mode, `scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py`, chars / 4, over `list_tools`; `--profile core` is new). Re-measured on 2026-11-17 after including the three live reads required by the links and worksets audit on main 1.5.0 (compact reads, paging and size cap are in the tree); the catalogue totals match the paging row above to the token, because those changes add no tool text beyond it and the core profile only filters:

| Profile | Tools | ~Tokens before | ~Tokens after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `full` | 302 | 80,191 | 80,191 |
| `daily` | 231 | 62,225 | 62,225 |
| `core` | 55 | not available | 14,151 |

Core is 82% smaller than full and 77% smaller than daily. It is still above 10k tokens, mostly the approval tools (about 1,000 for the first five; `policy_show` was added after these figures were measured), `revit_set_parameters`/`revit_get_parameters` (about 1,760) and the audits. Full and daily are unchanged, so no existing setup changes.

The family map is three lines in `SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS` (447 characters, about 112 tokens, sent once at initialisation, not part of the tool list). It names the prefixes and says a tool missing from the list is hidden by the startup profile and how to reach it (switch profile and restart). Instructions total 1,379 characters (about 345 tokens); the approval and Dev mode sentences are byte-for-byte unchanged and a test pins them. Core plus map is about 14,263 tokens.

What core keeps, and why (50 tools plus the approval tools):

| Family | Tools | Why |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Context and results | 4 | `revit_get_context` (Dev flag, document), `revit_health`, `revit_get_document_info`, `revit_get_result` for async answers |
| Jobs | 2 | `job_status`, `job_cancel`: follow and stop a long run |
| Snapshots | 4 | `snapshot_take`, `snapshot_query`, `snapshot_diff`: the before/after evidence; `snapshot_compute`: one-call answers over a snapshot |
| QA checks and issues | 5 | `qaqc_checker_run_check`, `list_issues`, `resolve_issue`, `list_rules`, `list_rule_packs`: the issue loop (pack import/export/validate stay hidden) |
| Review and checks | 4 | `revit_review`, `revit_warnings_delta`, `revit_check_levels_grids`, `revit_system_report`: composite read-only verdicts |
| Module audits | 7 | naming, doors and rooms, sheets and views, warnings triage, model bloat, links and worksets, `revit_cleanup_audit`: the routine coordinator audits |
| Element and project reads | 11 | list/inspect elements, element parameters, geometry, levels, views, families, categories, Revit links, link instances and worksets |
| Warnings and documents | 2 | `revit_get_warnings`, `revit_list_views_sheets_schedules` |
| Model inspector | 2 | summarize a model, inspect the selection |
| Parameters | 3 | `revit_get_parameters`, `revit_set_parameters` (the approved write path), `parameter_manager_filter_params` |
| Selection | 4 | get/set selection, select by unique ids, select by query: hand findings to the person in Revit |
| Power tools | 2 | `revit_execute_python` (anything not listed, still behind approval), `revit_api_lookup` (check an API before scripting) |

Left out on purpose: single-purpose creators (walls, sheets, views, MEP, sparing), exports, recipes, family editing, revisions, Rhino, Speckle, Navisworks, IFC and rule-pack admin. Reach them with `daily` or `full`. A user custom profile file can still narrow `core` but cannot hide approval tools.

Reproduce: `python scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py --profile core --output docs/mcp-token-measurement-after-core.json`. The command writes the evidence file. Measurement files are not kept in the repository.

## Follow-up: output schemas

Twenty read tools advertise an MCP `outputSchema` (`src/revit_mcp_server/output_schemas.py`). Each schema lists only the main top-level keys and their types, so it stays small. Same method as above (mock mode, `scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py`, chars / 4 over `list_tools`), measured with and without the schemas on the same tree:

| Profile | Tools | Characters without | Characters with | ~Tokens without | ~Tokens with |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `full` | 311 | 332,323 | 336,308 | 83,081 | 84,077 |
| `daily` | 240 | 260,460 | 264,445 | 65,115 | 66,111 |
| `core` | 57 | 59,612 | 63,522 | 14,903 | 15,881 |

The schemas add about 1,000 tokens in every profile (1.2% of full, 6.6% of core); 19 of the 20 tools are visible in `core` (all but `module_list_commands`). A successful call to one of these tools now carries its result twice: as text (unchanged) and as `structuredContent`. A client that passes only one of them to the model sees no change in response cost.

Every schema object now states `"additionalProperties": true` (about 30 characters per object, under 300 tokens in total; the table above predates it). Every successful reply of these tools carries `structuredContent`, because the Python SDK client rejects a reply without it. When a result does not match its schema, or the reply is a queued job, a call still running or a cursor page, the server sends a fallback object that validates: the result keys that match, required keys filled with empty values of their type, and `structured_fallback` with the reason and the filled and dropped keys. The text content holds the full result.

A later step added schemas for nine more core read tools whose result this server builds (`revit_warnings_delta`, `revit_get_parameters`, `naming_checker_check_names`, `sheet_view_audit_run_audit`, `schedule_consistency_check_doors_and_rooms`, `warnings_triage_review_warnings`, `links_worksets_audit_audit`, `model_inspector_inspect_selection`, `parameter_manager_filter_params`). Measured with `scripts/token_budget.py` on the same tree: `core` 70,054 to 72,813 characters (about +690 tokens, +3.9%), `daily` +2,759 characters, `full` +2,759 characters. All stay inside the 10% growth threshold of `docs/mcp-token-baseline.json`, so the baseline is unchanged. The 15 other read tools in `core` (`revit_health`, `revit_list_*`, `revit_get_*` and `revit_inspect_elements`) forward to the add-in and have no schema: their live shape is not built here and mock mode cannot show it. `tests/test_output_schemas.py` names them, so a new core read tool must either get a schema or be added to that list.

## Follow-up: deferred loading and the always-loaded set

A client with tool search can defer this server and keep a short always-loaded set: `ALWAYS_LOADED_TOOLS` in `tool_profiles.py` (`revit_get_context`, `snapshot_take`, `snapshot_compute`, `search_tools`, `context_report`, `plan_actions`, `execute_plan`, `list_pending_plans`). Setup: [deferred tool loading](deferred-tool-loading.md).

Same method as above (mock mode, chars / 4 over `list_tools`), with 313 tools, after `context_report` and the `_meta` always-load flag were added. `--always-loaded` measures only the always-loaded set. Names-only is the JSON list of tool names.

| Setup | Tools in prompt | ~Tokens of tool definitions |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `full`, no deferral | 313 | 86,877 |
| `daily`, no deferral | 242 | 68,639 |
| `core`, no deferral | 58 | 17,104 |
| Always-loaded set only (any profile) | 8 | 2,635 |
| `full` deferred, plus names of the 305 deferred tools | 8 + 305 names | about 4,550 |

With the Claude API tool search tool, deferred definitions are not in the prompt until a search returns them, so the startup cost is the always-loaded row plus the search tool itself. Claude Code lists the names of deferred tools at session start; the last row estimates that from names-only JSON (7,792 characters for all 313 names) and is not a measurement of Claude Code's own prompt. Neither row was measured in a live client. Server instructions (about 345 tokens) are sent in every setup.

Reproduce: `python scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py --always-loaded --output always-loaded.json`, and `--profile full|daily|core` for the other rows. `--only-tools a,b,c` measures any other subset.

## Follow-up: the `learned` profile

`MCP_REVIT_TOOL_PROFILE=learned` lists `core`, the always-loaded set and the 25 most used tools of the last 30 days from local usage counts, so a list fits what one person actually calls. It falls back to `daily` with fewer than 50 counted calls. `context_report` shows the most used tools and suggests `learned` when it would list at most 75% of the current list. Details and privacy: [learned profile](learned-profile.md).
## Follow-up: MCP Apps `_meta.ui`

For a client that declared the MCP Apps extension (`MCP_REVIT_MCP_APPS=auto`, the default) or with `MCP_REVIT_MCP_APPS=always`, `plan_actions` and `list_pending_plans` carry `_meta.ui.resourceUri` and every tool that is not read-only carries `_meta.ui.visibility: ["model"]` ([MCP Apps plan review view](mcp-apps.md)). Same method (mock mode, chars / 4 over `list_tools`, `full` profile, 314 listed tools): 343,087 characters without, 350,067 with, about 1,745 tokens more; 173 tools carry `_meta.ui`. Whether a client puts `_meta` in the model prompt depends on the client; UNVERIFIED. A client that does not declare the extension gets none of it in `auto` mode; `MCP_REVIT_MCP_APPS=off` removes it for every client.

## What dominates?

*Dated: 2026-11-05. The `module_list_commands` size below is from before the 2026-11-16 trims; see the follow-up sections above.*

Names-only JSON costs 7,538 characters (~1,885 tokens), versus 358,133 characters (~89,533 tokens) for the full schemas. Metadata originally adds 132,722 UTF-8 bytes (~33,181 tokens) over raw provider Tool definitions.

The assertion that plan echoes and results burn more than names is **partly confirmed**: `module_list_commands` alone costs ~13,924 tokens, exceeding every tool name combined (~1,885). The measured small parameter plan (~265 tokens) and four mock model reads (~76-93 tokens each) do not. The full schema catalogue dominates all these samples. No inference about real model result sizes or long script echoes is justified by these canned responses.

The sample plan request is 136 characters with one `revit_set_parameter_value` action, a 16-character value, and zero script characters. It creates a pending plan only. No approval or execution is performed. Its 590-character compact data payload expands to a 1,058-character serialized default response. The real module catalogue payload expands from 35,367 compact data characters to 55,697 serialized response characters.

The first probe also sampled health (197 response characters), document info (313), selection (305), one parameter value (385), and context (506). The definitive five-read benchmark below uses module commands, elements, families, element parameters, and views.

## Follow-up: large script-plan echoes

A second measurement, taken before the follow-up code changes, creates a pending
plan with a 16,384-character comment-only Python script. It never approves or
executes the plan. The script is echoed twice in the default plan structure:
`actions[].arguments.script` and `actions[].diff.after.script`.

| Payload | Before characters | After characters | Before ~tokens | After ~tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Compact script-plan response | 33,412 | 795 | 8,353 | 199 |
| Daily catalogue including the new option | 255,533 | 255,733 | 63,883 | 63,933 |

Request `response_options: {"compact": true, "omit_action_arguments": true}`
on `plan_actions` to omit these argument echoes from its returned summary.
This saves **97.62%** of the measured response, with a 50-token schema cost per
catalogue. The original script input cost remains. Default responses, stored
arguments, before evidence, complete review, plan hash and human approval rules
are preserved. The summary explicitly directs human review to the complete
stored plan; its hash identifies that full plan. Distinct after-state data,
errors and running-result diagnostics remain visible. This option does not
enable arbitrary plan field selection.

Evidence: `mcp-token-measurement-plan-script-before.json` (script fixture) and `mcp-token-measurement-plan-script-after.json` (same fixture with argument omission). The commands under Reproduce write them; they are not kept in the repository.

## Daily dependency audit

An offline search of the owner's own Dynamo automation scripts found no calls to the tools the daily profile hides. The calls they do make (context, Python, result collection, pending-plan creation and plan execution) remain available. The owner chose to retain used modules if discovered; this audit required no exceptions.

Profiles select provider/manifest IDs, including aliased commands. Native duct/pipe declarations carry explicit `revit_mep` ownership. Hidden direct calls, nested module calls and job targets are refused. Existing approved plans are preflighted before claiming any action; profile refusal preserves their approved state. The panel remains unrestricted and all exposed writes still require the existing approval process.

## Validation

*Dated: the 2026-11-05 implementation run.*

Initial implementation package suite: **2,747 passed, 150 skipped** in 190.28 seconds using
a project virtual environment. The two wheel-build tests
skip because `build` is not installed; browser, live-Revit and platform-specific
checks account for the other skips. No live Revit writes were performed.
Ruff passes on all changed Python files; `git diff --check` passes.
New coverage includes static full/daily/custom discovery, file/glob validation,
alias ownership, hidden direct and nested calls, untouched blocked approved
plans, human-only approval rules, redaction, default response compatibility,
opt-in projection/minification, and daily/custom subprocess MCP round trips.
The follow-up argument-echo change passes **109 targeted tests**, including
approval/review/hash invariants, default-response compatibility, invalid options,
error/progress preservation, and real MCP subprocess round trips. All changed
Python files pass Ruff. Independent review found no remaining concrete defects.

## Per-release measurement

Each release build runs `scripts/token_budget.py`, which measures the `core`, `daily` and `full`
catalogues and the representative mock calls, and attaches `token-budget.json` to the GitHub
release. The build fails when a profile's catalogue grows more than `threshold_pct` (10%) over
`docs/mcp-token-baseline.json`. When the growth is intended, run
`python scripts/token_budget.py --output token-budget.json --update-baseline` and commit the baseline.

## Reproduce

```powershell
& python scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py --profile full --output docs/mcp-token-measurement-after-full.json
& python scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py --profile full --compact-read-results --project-module-commands --output docs/mcp-token-measurement-after-compact.json
& python scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py --profile daily --compact-read-results --project-module-commands --output docs/mcp-token-measurement-after-daily.json
& python scripts/measure_mcp_tokens.py --profile daily --compact-read-results --plan-script-chars 16384 --omit-plan-arguments --output docs/mcp-token-measurement-plan-script-after.json
```

To reproduce the original baseline, run the initial measurement script against the original source commit. Optional `--profile-file` accepts a custom include/exclude file. Each run records its Git HEAD and settings; after snapshots were captured on the working tree during implementation.

Evidence: the JSON files the commands above write (before, after full, after compact, after daily). They are not kept in the repository; earlier copies are in the commit history.

=== FILE: docs/performance.md ===

# Server start-up and bridge client performance

All numbers on this page are mock-mode measurements of the Python MCP server (`MCP_REVIT_MODE=mock`). No Revit was involved; they do not describe live Revit calls. See [ADR 0007](adr/0007-hub-performance-posture.md) for the performance rules.

## Method

- Linux container, Python 3.13, the project virtual environment, an empty temporary workspace, no APS, Speckle or proxy settings.
- "Before" runs the previous source tree, "after" runs the current one, on the same interpreter and installed packages. Runs alternate between the two; the table shows the median.
- Phase times come from one fresh process per run: import `revit_mcp_server.mcp_server`, call `build_registry()`, call `list_tools()` once.
- "Spawn to list_tools" starts `python -m revit_mcp_server` over stdio with the MCP Python client, sends `initialize`, then `tools/list`, and stops the clock at the reply.
- Absolute numbers depend on the machine. Compare the before and after columns only.
- The table was measured on an idle machine with the 1.5.1 tree as "before". A repeat with the 1.6 tree as "before" on a loaded machine showed the same direction: spawn to `tools/list` 1,326 ms to 856 ms, `build_registry()` 589 ms to 65 ms (medians).

## Cold start (mock mode)

| Measure (median) | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Spawn to `tools/list` reply, stdio (9 runs) | 825 ms | 575 ms |
| Import `revit_mcp_server.mcp_server` (11 runs) | 449 ms | 426 ms |
| `build_registry()` | 231 ms | 38 ms |
| First `list_tools()` | 8 ms | 11 ms |
| Whole process, import to first `list_tools()` | 912 ms | 632 ms |
| Modules loaded after `list_tools()` | 1,040 | 711 |

## What changed

- `openpyxl` (which loads `numpy`) is imported by `report_generator` only when a tool writes a workbook. `param_completeness` loads `report_generator` at start, so this import ran on every start before.
- `yaml` is imported by `qaqc_checker` and `recipe_runner` only when a rule pack or recipe is read.
- The Speckle and Autodesk Data providers build their `httpx.AsyncClient` on first request. Each client loads the system CA bundle (about 10 ms), and three were built at start.
- The module registry reads the installed package version once instead of once per module (32 metadata file parses).

`specklepy`, `ifcopenshell` and `networkx` were already lazy. Tests check that importing the server and building the registry load none of `specklepy`, `ifcopenshell`, `networkx`, `openpyxl`, `numpy` or `yaml`, and build no `httpx.AsyncClient` (`tests/test_lazy_imports_and_client_reuse.py`).

## What remains

- About 420 ms of the import is the MCP Python SDK itself (`mcp.server` loads FastMCP, Starlette, Uvicorn, Pydantic and httpx). The server cannot skip it.
- The server's own modules add about 60 ms on top of the SDK.

## Result JSON

`orjson` was not added. `json.dumps` of a 200 KB result takes about 2 ms here, and read-only results are capped at 20,000 characters by default (`max_chars`). The gain would not be measurable in a tool call.

## Bridge client

- `BridgeClient` sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip`. httpx decodes a gzip body before `.json()`, so an add-in that compresses large responses needs no other client change. Plain bodies still work.
- Panel hub routing keeps one cached client per Revit (endpoint and session token). Building a client and its network initialise run outside the cache lock. A cached client is dropped when its Revit's registry entry is gone, or after its `/health` probe fails three times in a row following failed calls (`bridge/routing.py`).

## Add-in timings

`revit_perf_report` reads the add-in's `/health` and lists per-command `count`, `p50_ms`, `p95_ms`, `max_ms` and `avg_bytes`, sorted by p95, with `queue_depth`. An add-in without a `timings` field is reported as older, not as an error. In mock mode the tool returns sample numbers marked `mock: true`.

UNVERIFIED: the `timings` field and gzip responses come from a separate add-in change. Neither was observed against a live Revit for this page.

=== FILE: docs/deferred-tool-loading.md ===

# Deferred tool loading

The full tool list is about 83k tokens and `core` about 15k (see [MCP token budget](mcp-token-budget.md)). A client with tool search can leave most tool definitions out of the prompt and load each one when a search returns it. The prompt prefix then stays small and cacheable.

This page shows how to defer the AEC Model Bridge server and keep a short always-loaded set. Deferral changes what the model sees, not what the server allows. Every write still needs a plan that a person approves.

## The always-loaded set

These eight tools stay loaded. The list is `ALWAYS_LOADED_TOOLS` in `packages/mcp-server-revit/src/revit_mcp_server/tool_profiles.py`, and a test pins it.

| Tool | Why it stays loaded |
| --- | --- |
| `revit_get_context` | Mode, Dev flag and document at the start of every task |
| `snapshot_take` | One capture of the model for later questions |
| `snapshot_compute` | Answers over a snapshot in one call |
| `search_tools` | Finds any tool, including tools the profile hides |
| `context_report` | Profile, tool count and tool-list size |
| `plan_actions` | Drafts the plan for any write |
| `execute_plan` | Runs a plan after a person approves it |
| `list_pending_plans` | Plan state |

All eight are visible in the `core`, `daily` and `full` profiles. Together they are about 2,635 tokens.

In `tools/list` the server marks each of these tools with `"_meta": {"anthropic/alwaysLoad": true}`. No other tool carries the flag.

## Claude Code

Claude Code turns tool search on by default: MCP tools are deferred and Claude searches for them. A tool whose `_meta` has `"anthropic/alwaysLoad": true` loads up front. So the default plugin or `claude mcp add` setup already defers the server and keeps the eight tools loaded. No extra setting is needed.

The plugin's `.mcp.json` (unchanged, shown for reference):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "aec-model-bridge": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "--from",
        "git+https://github.com/Sam-AEC/aec-model-bridge#subdirectory=packages/mcp-server-revit",
        "aec-model-bridge"
      ],
      "env": {
        "MCP_REVIT_MODE": "bridge"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Settings that change this, from the Claude Code MCP docs:

- Leave `alwaysLoad` out of the server entry. With `"alwaysLoad": true` every tool of the server loads up front. With `"alwaysLoad": false` every tool is deferred, including the eight marked ones (Claude Code v2.1.287 or later).
- `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH`: unset or `true` defers MCP tools. `auto` or `auto:N` defers only when tool definitions pass 10% (or N%) of the context window. `false` loads every tool up front.
- On models earlier than Claude Opus 4 and Sonnet 4, on some Google Cloud Agent Platform models and on Microsoft Foundry deployments hosted on Azure, Claude Code loads every tool up front.
- Run `/context` to see which tools are loaded and which are deferred.

Combine deferral with a profile when the client cannot defer: `MCP_REVIT_TOOL_PROFILE=core` in `env` lists about 58 tools.

UNVERIFIED: the `_meta` flag and the deferral behaviour were checked against the Claude Code docs, not observed in a live Claude Code session with this server.

## Claude API

This server speaks MCP over stdio on the machine that runs Revit. The API's MCP connector (`mcp_servers` and `mcp_toolset`) only reaches servers exposed over public HTTPS, so it cannot start this server. Do not expose the Revit bridge to the internet for this.

Use your own MCP client instead: start the server, read `tools/list`, and pass the tools to the Messages API with the tool search tool. Set `defer_loading: true` on every tool except the always-loaded set. At least one tool must stay non-deferred; the tool search tool itself must never be deferred.

```python
import anthropic

ALWAYS_LOADED = {
    "revit_get_context", "snapshot_take", "snapshot_compute", "search_tools",
    "context_report", "plan_actions", "execute_plan", "list_pending_plans",
}


def to_api_tools(mcp_tools):
    """mcp_tools: the Tool list from an MCP ClientSession.list_tools() call."""
    tools = [{"type": "tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_bm25"}]
    for tool in mcp_tools:
        entry = {
            "name": tool.name,
            "description": tool.description or "",
            "input_schema": tool.inputSchema,
        }
        if tool.name not in ALWAYS_LOADED:
            entry["defer_loading"] = True
        tools.append(entry)
    return tools


client = anthropic.Anthropic()
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    tools=to_api_tools(mcp_tools),
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How many doors on Level 1 have no fire rating?"}],
)
```

Notes from the tool search docs:

- Send every tool definition on every request, deferred ones included. The API needs them to run the search and expand `tool_reference` blocks.
- Pass the assistant content back unchanged, including `server_tool_use` and `tool_search_tool_result` blocks. Never return a `tool_result` for a `srvtoolu_...` id.
- A deferred tool cannot also carry `cache_control`. Put the cache breakpoint on a non-deferred tool.
- `tool_search_tool_regex_20251119` is the regex variant; the BM25 variant takes natural-language queries.
- When Claude calls a tool, run it through your MCP session with `call_tool` and return the result as a `tool_result`. The server's approval gate applies to those calls as to any other client.

If you run the server behind your own remote HTTPS MCP endpoint (not shipped by this project), the connector shape is one `mcp_toolset` that defers the server and keeps the eight tools loaded, with the beta header `mcp-client-2025-11-20`:

```json
{
  "mcp_servers": [
    {"type": "url", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp", "name": "aec-model-bridge"}
  ],
  "tools": [
    {"type": "tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_bm25"},
    {
      "type": "mcp_toolset",
      "mcp_server_name": "aec-model-bridge",
      "default_config": {"defer_loading": true},
      "configs": {
        "revit_get_context": {"defer_loading": false},
        "snapshot_take": {"defer_loading": false},
        "snapshot_compute": {"defer_loading": false},
        "search_tools": {"defer_loading": false},
        "context_report": {"defer_loading": false},
        "plan_actions": {"defer_loading": false},
        "execute_plan": {"defer_loading": false},
        "list_pending_plans": {"defer_loading": false}
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

UNVERIFIED: neither snippet was run against the live API with this server. The field names come from the tool search and MCP connector docs.

## Two searches

The client's tool search finds deferred tools that the profile lists. The server's `search_tools` searches every registered tool and says which profile shows a hidden one. Both return exact tool names, and a client calls a tool by that name. A tool that the profile hides is never in `tools/list`, so client tool search cannot find it; `search_tools` can, and its `note` tells the person how to switch profile.

## Other clients

Codex, Cursor and other MCP clients: UNVERIFIED. Where a client has no deferral, use `MCP_REVIT_TOOL_PROFILE=core`.

=== FILE: docs/python-automation.md ===

# Python automation in Revit

How to write fast `revit_execute_python` scripts, and the `amb` helper library that the server can put before a script. The approval rules do not change: `mode='read'` needs no approval and cannot open transactions; `mode='write'` (the default) needs an approved plan.

Status: the helpers and the patterns below have not run in a live Revit session (UNVERIFIED). Server-side behaviour (when the prelude is added, read-mode checks) is covered by `tests/test_python_helpers.py`.

## Engines and syntax

The add-in runs IronPython 2.7 on Revit 2024 (net48) and IronPython 3.4 on Revit 2025 and later (net8, net10). A script that must run on both uses the shared subset:

- No f-strings. Use `"%d walls" % n` or `"{0} walls".format(n)`.
- `print(x)` with one argument only. `print(a, b)` prints a tuple on 2.7.
- No annotations, keyword-only arguments, `nonlocal`, `yield from` or `a, *b = ...`.
- No `long`, `basestring`, `unicode` or `xrange` (missing on 3.4); no `json` module on some 2.7 builds.
- Use `//` for whole-number division.

Check any API member you have not used before with `revit_api_lookup`.

## Turning the helpers on

```json
{"script": "print(amb.count(amb.instances('Walls')))", "mode": "read", "helpers": true}
```

- `helpers: true` puts the helper text before the script. Without it nothing is added.
- Read mode gets the read part only (`python_helpers/amb_read.ipy`). The server checks the caller's script, then checks the combined text again. The add-in repeats its own text check and keeps its roll-back guard. A read-mode script that names `Transaction` is refused with or without helpers.
- Write mode also gets the write part (`python_helpers/amb_write.ipy`): batched transactions, sub-transactions and transaction groups.
- Error line numbers count the helper lines. The helpers end with a marker line `# ---- end of AEC Model Bridge helpers (amb) ...`; the caller's script starts on the next line.
- A script with `from __future__ import ...` is refused when `helpers` is true, because that import must be the first statement.
- `revit_run_job` takes the same `helpers` flag for scripts.
- Saved recipes (`revit_recipe_run`) always get the read part; a recipe that runs as write also gets the write part.

## Read helpers

All helpers are static methods of `amb`. Lengths are Revit internal units (feet) unless a unit is named.

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `amb.instances(cats, view=None)` | Placed elements of one or more categories: `OfCategory` or `ElementMulticategoryFilter`, then `WhereElementIsNotElementType` |
| `amb.types(cats)` | Element types of one or more categories |
| `amb.of_class(cls, view=None)` | `OfClass` collector |
| `amb.collector(view=None, ids=None)` | Plain collector over the document, one view, or a set of ids |
| `amb.ids(col)` / `amb.count(col)` / `amb.first(col)` / `amb.take(col, n)` | Results without loading every element |
| `amb.where(col, param, op, value)` | One `ElementParameterFilter` rule |
| `amb.rule(...)` / `amb.where_all(col, rules)` | Several rules that must all match |
| `amb.in_box(col, lo, hi, inside=False)` | `BoundingBoxIntersectsFilter` or `BoundingBoxIsInsideFilter` |
| `amb.near_point(col, pt)` | `BoundingBoxContainsPointFilter` |
| `amb.intersecting_solid(col, solid)` / `amb.intersecting_element(col, e)` | `ElementIntersectsSolidFilter` / `ElementIntersectsElementFilter` |
| `amb.solids(e)` / `amb.box_solid(lo, hi)` | Solids of an element; a transient box solid |
| `amb.to_internal(v, unit)` / `amb.from_internal(v, unit)` | `UnitUtils` with `UnitTypeId` (`mm`, `cm`, `m`, `ft`, `in`, `m2`, `ft2`, `m3`, `ft3`, `deg`, `rad`) |
| `amb.dependents(e, element_filter=None)` | `Element.GetDependentElements` as integer ids |
| `amb.value(e, param, unit=None)` / `amb.parameter(e, param)` | Parameter value by storage type |
| `amb.eid(x)` / `amb.element_id(x)` / `amb.id_list(ids)` | Ids across Revit versions (`ElementId.Value` on 2024+) |
| `amb.bic(name)` | `'Walls'`, `'OST_Walls'` or `'Structural Framing'` to `BuiltInCategory` |

`param` is a `BuiltInParameter`, its name (`'ALL_MODEL_INSTANCE_COMMENTS'`), an `ElementId`, or a project or shared parameter name. `op` is one of `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `contains`, `not_contains`, `begins`, `not_begins`, `ends`, `not_ends`, `has_value`, `no_value`. A float value compares with `epsilon` (default `1e-6`, internal units). Pass a float for a length, area or angle parameter (`3.0`, not `3`): an int value builds an integer rule, which does not match a double parameter. Text rules use the two-argument factory methods of Revit 2023 and later (not case sensitive) and fall back to the older overload.

## Write helpers (write mode only)

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `amb.run(name, fn, *args)` | `fn` in one transaction; commit on return, roll back and re-raise on error |
| `amb.batch(name, items, fn, max_failures=None)` | All items in one transaction, each in its own `SubTransaction`; returns `(done, failed)` |
| `amb.try_sub(fn, *args)` | `fn` in a `SubTransaction` inside an open transaction; returns `(True, result)` or `(False, message)` |
| `amb.group(name, [(step, fn), ...])` | Each step in its own transaction inside a `TransactionGroup` that is assimilated into one undo entry |
| `amb.set(e, param, value, unit=None)` | Set a parameter by storage type, converting a unit first |
| `amb.regenerate()` | `doc.Regenerate()` once after a batch |

Transactions come from `amb_transaction(doc, name)`, which the add-in defines in write mode: warnings are dismissed without a dialog and returned in the result's `warnings`, and errors roll the transaction back. If it is missing, the helpers use a plain `Transaction` with their own `IFailuresPreprocessor` set through `FailureHandlingOptions`.

## Patterns and why they are faster

### Quick filters first, then slow filters

Revit checks quick filters (category, class, element type flag, bounding box) against element records without loading the element. Slow filters (parameter rules, solid intersection) load each element. Apply quick filters first so the slow filter sees fewer elements.

```python
col = amb.instances(["Walls", "Floors"])             # quick
col = amb.in_box(col, (0, 0, 0), (50, 50, 12))       # quick
col = amb.where(col, "ALL_MODEL_INSTANCE_COMMENTS", "begins", "AMB_")  # slow, now on fewer elements
print(amb.count(col))
```

### Ids, not elements

`ToElements()` and iterating a collector build one Python wrapper per element. `ToElementIds()`, `GetElementCount()` and `FirstElement()` do not. Fetch elements only for the ids you print or change.

```python
ids = amb.ids(amb.instances("Doors"))
print(len(ids))
for e in amb.elements(ids[:20]):
    print(e.Name)
```

### Filter parameters inside Revit

A Python loop that reads a parameter on every element crosses the .NET boundary twice per element. An `ElementParameterFilter` runs the comparison in native code.

```python
# Walls taller than 3 m
tall = amb.where(amb.instances("Walls"), "WALL_USER_HEIGHT_PARAM", ">", amb.to_internal(3.0, "m"))
```

The same rule without the helpers:

```python
from Autodesk.Revit.DB import *
provider = ParameterValueProvider(ElementId(BuiltInParameter.WALL_USER_HEIGHT_PARAM))
rule = FilterDoubleRule(provider, FilterNumericGreater(), 3.0 / 0.3048, 1e-6)
walls = FilteredElementCollector(doc).OfCategory(BuiltInCategory.OST_Walls) \
    .WhereElementIsNotElementType().WherePasses(ElementParameterFilter(rule))
```

### Spatial filters

`BoundingBoxIntersectsFilter` and `BoundingBoxIsInsideFilter` are quick filters. `ElementIntersectsSolidFilter` tests real geometry and is slow, so narrow with a box first.

```python
lo, hi = (0, 0, 0), (30, 30, 10)
near = amb.in_box(amb.instances(["Ducts", "Pipes"]), lo, hi)
hits = amb.intersecting_solid(near, amb.box_solid(lo, hi))
```

### One transaction for many changes

Each transaction regenerates the model and adds an undo entry. One transaction for a batch regenerates once. A `SubTransaction` per item lets one bad item roll back alone.

```python
ids = amb.ids(amb.where(amb.instances("Doors"), "ALL_MODEL_INSTANCE_COMMENTS", "no_value"))
done, failed = amb.batch("Tag doors", amb.elements(ids),
                         lambda e: amb.set(e, "ALL_MODEL_INSTANCE_COMMENTS", "AMB_CHECKED"))
print("%d set, %d failed" % (len(done), len(failed)))
```

Use `amb.group` when steps must be separate transactions (for example a regenerate between them) but should undo as one.

### Units

`UnitUtils.ConvertToInternalUnits(value, UnitTypeId.Millimeters)` replaces hand-written factors and covers areas, volumes and angles. `amb.mm(v)` divides by 304.8 without a Revit call for tight loops.

### Dependent elements

`Element.GetDependentElements(filter)` returns hosted and owned elements (doors in a wall, tags, sketch lines) in one call. Use it before deleting or moving an element to see what goes with it.

```python
wall = amb.first(amb.instances("Walls"))
print(amb.dependents(wall, amb.category_filter(["Doors", "Windows"])))
```

## Keep scripts short

A script runs on Revit's user-interface thread and cannot be cancelled. Keep each call well under 20 seconds, work from ids, and split long work over several calls or `revit_run_job`.

## Script lint (advisory)

`revit_execute_python` checks the script text for known Revit API and IronPython traps (`revit_mcp_server/script_lint.py`). The warnings only inform. They never block, change or delay a script, and read mode and the approval gate are unchanged.

- `execute_tool` adds `lint_warnings` to the result of a `revit_execute_python` call: a list of `{rule, line, message, example}`.
- `plan_actions` listings add `script_lint` and a "Script lint" section in `preview_markdown` for each `revit_execute_python` action. Both are computed when the plan is shown, so they are not part of the plan hash.
- Rules: `collections_import`, `fstring`, `out_parameter_roof`, `wall_flip`, `phase_indexer`, `transaction_unclosed`, `family_doc_not_closed_in_finally`, `dialog_blocks_bridge`, `long_sleep`.

The rules are text matches and can warn about code that is fine. They were written from traps seen in live use and tested on fixture scripts only. UNVERIFIED in live Revit.

## Recipes that use the helpers

Two read-only starter recipes use `amb`: `elements_by_parameter` (one category plus one parameter rule) and `elements_in_box` (categories plus a box in metres). See [recipes-library.md](recipes-library.md).

## Related

- [ADR 0019](adr/0019-optional-cpython-engine.md): optional CPython 3 engine for numpy and pandas (proposal).
- [Recipe library](recipes-library.md): saved scripts with checked parameters.
- [Security model](security.md): what read mode does and does not protect.

=== FILE: docs/snapshot-compute.md ===

# snapshot_compute: one-call model queries

`snapshot_compute` runs a read-only pipeline over a saved snapshot and returns only the result. Use it when a question would otherwise take many list, inspect or parameter calls. It follows the pattern of composing tool work in one request and keeping intermediate rows out of the model context, without running model-written code.

Take a snapshot first with `snapshot_take` (scope it with `categories` on large models), then pass its `snapshot_id`.

## Pipeline

`steps` is a list of up to 12 objects, run in order. Each step can have:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Step name. Later steps read it as `$name`. Default `stepN`. |
| `from` | `elements` (default), `types`, `relations`, `$<earlier step>` or `link:<snapshot_id>` (see Linked snapshots). |
| `join` | List of `type`, `host`, `level`, `room`, `group`, `hosted`, `relation_out`, `relation_in`, or `{"rel": ..., "as": ..., "kind": ...}`. The related record is added under `as` (default the join name). `hosted` and the relation joins add a list of up to 50 elements. |
| `spatial` | `{"with": "$<earlier step>", "test": ..., "distance": feet, "as": name}`. Adds the rows of that step whose bounding box passes the test (see Spatial joins). |
| `where` | `{"field", "op", "value", "ci"}`, a list (all must match), or `{"all": [...]}`, `{"any": [...]}`, `{"not": {...}}`. Ops: `eq`, `ne`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `in`, `nin`, `contains`, `startswith`, `endswith`, `exists`, `empty`. `value: {"field": "path"}` compares two fields of the same row. |
| `group_by` | Path or list of paths. |
| `aggregate` | `{"name": {"op", "field"}}` with `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `distinct`, `list`. Without `group_by` it returns one row. |
| `sort` | Path, `{"field", "desc"}` or a list of them. Numbers sort before text; missing values last. |
| `select` | List of paths or `{"field", "as"}`. |
| `limit` | Rows kept by the step. |

A step runs its parts in this order: `from`, `join`, `spatial`, `where`, `group_by` and `aggregate`, `sort`, `select`, `limit`. So `where` can test join and spatial results, and rows are narrowed before a spatial join only in an earlier step.

Top level: `steps` or `query` (one of them); `params` (with `query` only); `return` names the step to return (default the last, or the saved query's `return`); `max_rows` (1 to 1000, default 100) caps rows in the reply while `row_count` gives the total.

Paths are dotted. A parameter yields its value: `params.Mark`, `host.params.Fire Rating`, `type.params.Width`, `location.xyz.2`, `bbox.max.0`.

Numbers compare as numbers, including numeric text such as `"60"`. A comparison between a number and non-numeric text does not match.

## Examples

Doors rated lower than their host wall:

```json
{"snapshot_id": "01J...", "steps": [{
  "join": ["host"],
  "where": [
    {"field": "category", "value": "OST_Doors"},
    {"field": "params.Fire Rating", "op": "lt", "value": {"field": "host.params.Fire Rating"}}
  ],
  "select": [{"field": "params.Mark", "as": "door"}, {"field": "host.params.Fire Rating", "as": "wall"}]
}]}
```

Door count and marks per level:

```json
{"snapshot_id": "01J...", "steps": [
  {"name": "doors", "where": {"field": "category", "value": "OST_Doors"}, "join": ["level"]},
  {"from": "$doors", "group_by": ["level.type_name"],
   "aggregate": {"n": "count", "marks": {"op": "list", "field": "params.Mark"}}}
]}
```

Rooms with no number, largest first:

```json
{"snapshot_id": "01J...", "steps": [{
  "where": [{"field": "category", "value": "OST_Rooms"}, {"field": "params.Number", "op": "empty"}],
  "sort": {"field": "params.Area", "desc": true}, "select": ["uid", "name", "params.Area"]
}]}
```

## Spatial joins

`spatial` compares each row's `bbox` with the `bbox` of every row of an earlier step and adds the matches under `as` (default the earlier step's name), at most 50, plus `<as>_count` with the full number.

| `test` | A row matches when |
|---|---|
| `overlaps` | the two boxes share any point (touching counts). |
| `contains` | the row's box holds the other box. |
| `within` | the row's box lies inside the other box. |
| `within_distance` | the gap between the boxes is at most `distance` (0 to 1000). The gap is 0 when the boxes overlap. |

- Distances are in the snapshot's `bbox` units. Revit's internal unit is feet; that the add-in writes `bbox` in feet is UNVERIFIED in a live Revit.
- A row without a valid `bbox` (missing, not three numbers, or min above max) never matches. `select` drops `bbox`, so keep it in steps a later spatial join reads.
- An element never matches itself (same `uid` and same `_snapshot_id`).
- The number of comparisons is rows with a box times `with` rows with a box. Above 250,000 the step is refused; narrow both sides with `where` in earlier steps.
- Bounding boxes are axis-aligned and larger than the element, so results are candidates, not exact clashes.

Doors whose boxes touch more than one wall:

```json
{"snapshot_id": "01J...", "steps": [
  {"name": "walls", "where": {"field": "category", "value": "OST_Walls"}},
  {"name": "doors", "where": {"field": "category", "value": "OST_Doors"}},
  {"from": "$doors", "spatial": {"with": "$walls", "test": "overlaps", "as": "walls"},
   "where": {"field": "walls_count", "op": "gt", "value": 1},
   "select": ["params.Mark", "walls_count", {"field": "walls.0.uid", "as": "first_wall"}]}
]}
```

## Linked snapshots

`from: "link:<snapshot_id>"` reads the elements of another saved snapshot in the same workspace, for example a snapshot taken in a linked model. Use it to compare a host and a link in one call.

- Each row from a link carries `_snapshot_id`. Host rows do not.
- Joins on link rows (`type`, `host`, `hosted`, relations) look up records in that link's snapshot.
- At most 4 linked snapshots per call. Reading the same link in several steps counts once.
- The id is checked like `snapshot_id`: a plain name of a file in `<workspace>/snapshots/`. A missing or invalid snapshot is refused with the step name.
- The reply lists `linked_snapshots`. `partial_snapshot` is true when the host or any link is partial.
- No link transform is applied. Spatial joins between host and link rows are only meaningful when both snapshots share coordinates (UNVERIFIED for snapshots taken from live linked models).

Walls of the host that overlap walls of a link:

```json
{"snapshot_id": "01J...HOST", "steps": [
  {"name": "link_walls", "from": "link:01J...LINK", "where": {"field": "category", "value": "OST_Walls"}},
  {"name": "host_walls", "where": {"field": "category", "value": "OST_Walls"}},
  {"from": "$host_walls", "spatial": {"with": "$link_walls", "test": "overlaps", "as": "clash"},
   "where": {"field": "clash_count", "op": "gt", "value": 0}, "select": ["uid", "clash_count"]}
]}
```

## Saved queries

`query: "<name>"` runs the pipeline in `<workspace>/queries/<name>.json` instead of `steps`. Names use letters, digits, `_` and `-`, without `.json`; paths are refused. The file is at most 256,000 bytes. Write it with any file tool; there is no separate tool for it.

The file is a list of steps, or an object:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `steps` | Required. Steps as above. |
| `return` | Step to return. The call's `return` takes precedence. |
| `params` | Default values for params. |
| `description` | Text for people. |

`{"$param": "name"}` anywhere in `steps` is replaced by the whole JSON value of that param from the call's `params`, or else from the file's `params`. Text is never templated: `"$param"` inside a string stays as it is, and a param value is not searched for more `$param`. The result is checked exactly like inline steps.

Refused: a missing or unreadable file, invalid JSON, unknown top-level keys, a `$param` with no value, a call param the steps do not use, more than 20 params, and param names other than letters, digits and `_`.

`<workspace>/queries/doors_by_mark.json`:

```json
{"description": "Doors whose Mark is in a list.",
 "params": {"category": "OST_Doors"},
 "steps": [{"where": [
   {"field": "category", "value": {"$param": "category"}},
   {"field": "params.Mark", "op": "in", "value": {"$param": "marks"}}
 ], "select": ["uid", "params.Mark"]}]}
```

Call: `{"snapshot_id": "01J...", "query": "doors_by_mark", "params": {"marks": ["D-101", "D-102"]}}`.

## Rule packs

A QA/QC rule can be a pipeline: the rule field `pipeline` holds steps, and each row of the last step is an issue. See [rule-packs.md](rule-packs.md).

## Taking smaller or faster snapshots

`snapshot_take` options that reduce what the add-in reads (issues #289, #290):

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `categories` | Read only these categories, for example `["Doors", "Rooms"]`. |
| `params` | Read only these parameters (up to 100 names such as `"Mark"`, or built-in ids such as `ALL_MODEL_MARK`). The snapshot records `counts.params`, and QA modules treat it as partial for checks that read other parameters. |
| `slice_size` | 10 to 5000. Read about this many elements per Revit turn and assemble the slices into one snapshot. If the model changes between slices, the reply has `changed_during_capture: true`. |
| `base_snapshot_id` | Incremental capture. The add-in re-reads only elements changed since that snapshot (and instances of changed types), lists every element in scope, and the server merges the result with the base into a new full snapshot. |

An incremental capture falls back to a full capture, and says why in `incremental_reason`, when:

- the base is partial (truncated, dirty-only) or was taken with other `categories` or `params`;
- the base has no change-journal position (mock mode or an older add-in);
- the add-in's change journal does not cover the base: another document, a reopen, reload, sync with central, save as, a Revit restart, or a journal that grew past its entry limit;
- the add-in does not return an incremental capture (older add-in);
- the delta cannot be merged (another document, cut short, or an element missing from both).

Whether slices and incremental captures are faster than a full capture on a real model is UNVERIFIED in a live Revit. Whether the change journal sees every change (for example from links, worksharing or undo) is also UNVERIFIED.

## Limits and safety

- Read-only. It reads snapshot and query files in the workspace and never calls Revit.
- No expressions, code or regular expressions are evaluated. Unknown keys, ops, joins, spatial tests and aggregates are refused with a message that names the step.
- At most 12 steps, 50 clauses per `all` or `any`, 6 nesting levels, 50 items per list aggregate, list join or spatial match list, 500 characters per text value, 4 linked snapshots, 250,000 spatial comparisons per step.
- `partial_snapshot: true` means the snapshot hit its size limit or was taken with `params`, so it does not cover the whole model or every parameter.
- Element-to-room joins read `room_uids`, which the add-in extractor does not fill for every element (UNVERIFIED in a live Revit).

=== FILE: docs/read-cursors.md ===

# Read result cursors

A read-only tool result longer than the size cap is cut at list rows. The answer says how much was left out and how to get the rest. Write tools, plans, proofs, approvals, jobs and errors are never cut.

## The cap

- Default: 20,000 characters of result JSON (`DEFAULT_MAX_CHARS`).
- Server-wide: `MCP_REVIT_READ_MAX_CHARS` (characters, `0` = off). Read on each call.
- Per call: `response_options.max_chars` (`0` = off). It overrides the server value.
- The largest list in the result is cut first, at a row boundary. The answer stays valid JSON.

## A cut answer

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `truncated` | `true` when rows were left out. |
| `total` | Rows in the full list. |
| `returned` | Rows in this answer. |
| `truncated_field` | Dotted path of the list that was cut, for example `elements` or `data.rows`. |
| `also_trimmed` | Other lists that were cut, with their counts. Only the first list pages. |
| `cursor` | Opaque string for the next part. |
| `next` | One line on how to use `cursor` or `resource_uri`. |
| `resource_uri` | Present instead of `cursor` when the list was too large to keep in memory. |

When the result already has a key with one of these names, the markers move under `truncation`.

## Next part

Repeat the same tool with the same arguments and `fields`, and add the cursor:

```json
{"category": "Walls", "response_options": {"cursor": "rc...-120"}}
```

- The server returns the next rows from memory. The tool is not run again, so Revit is not asked twice.
- The part holds the cut list only, at its path, with `truncated`, `total`, `offset`, `returned` and, when rows remain, a new `cursor`.
- `max_chars` and `compact` may change between parts. Each part holds at least one row.
- A cursor can be repeated until it expires.

## Refusals

A cursor is refused with kind `invalid_cursor` and a plain message when:

- it expired. Cursors last `MCP_REVIT_READ_CURSOR_TTL` seconds (default 600, at most 3600);
- the server restarted. Cursors live only in the server process;
- the tool, arguments or `fields` differ from the call that issued it;
- it is malformed or points past the end.

Call the tool again without a cursor to start over.

## Storage limits

- At most 32 cursors, and about 16 million characters in total. The oldest go first.
- A cut list longer than 2 million characters is not kept in memory. The full redacted result is saved to `<workspace>/results/<id>.json` and the answer carries `resource_uri` (`aec://result/<id>`) plus an MCP resource link. Read it with `resources/read`.
- Only the newest 20 saved results are kept. Ids are checked with `safe_child`, so a link resolves only inside the workspace `results` folder.
- Saved and stored results are the redacted answer, never the raw provider output.

## Where it applies

Every read-only tool, including `revit_list_elements`, `revit_list_views`, `revit_list_families`, `revit_get_element_parameters`, `module_list_commands` and `snapshot_compute`. The five tools in `READERS` advertise `cursor` in their `response_options` schema; other read-only tools accept it without listing it. The list tools that take `limit` and `offset` still page in the provider; cursors page what the size cap cut.

Behaviour against a live Revit is UNVERIFIED; tests use mock and stub providers.

=== FILE: packages/claude-plugin/skills/aec-model-bridge/SKILL.md ===

---
name: aec-model-bridge
description: How to operate the AEC Model Bridge Revit MCP server with few calls and small results. Use at the start of any task that reads or changes a Revit model through AEC Model Bridge tools. Covers context and approval mode, tool profiles, finding tools, snapshot queries, compact output, plans and error kinds.
---

# Operate AEC Model Bridge efficiently

AEC Model Bridge exposes a Revit model through MCP tools. Writes go through
plans that a person approves. This skill keeps calls few and results small.
For the review and approval steps in detail, also use the `revit-review` skill
when it is installed.

## 1. Read context once

Call `revit_get_context` once at the start of a task. Read from `server`:

- `server.dev_mode`: when true, the person enabled Dev mode for this session.
  Write tools are called directly, with no plan. Stay inside the scope the
  person gave and verify every change.
- `server.approval_mode`: `look_only` allows reads only. `ask_first` needs a
  plan that a person approves before any write. `auto` is a time-limited window
  that a person opened in the panel.
- `server.plans_required`, when present: when true, every write needs a plan,
  whatever the other fields say.

Do not call it again unless the person says Revit, the document or the mode
changed. If it reports `mock: true`, the data is sample data. Say so in every
report.

## 2. Know the profile

The server starts with one tool profile: `core` (smallest), `daily` or
`full` (all tools). A tool that the profile hides is not listed and is refused
with kind `tool_profile_blocked`. Only the person can change the profile and
restart the server.

Call `context_report` when you need the active profile, the listed tool count
or the context cost of the tool list. It also gives tips to use less.

## 3. Search before you guess

Do not guess tool names. Call `search_tools` with a few words, for example
`{"query": "door fire rating", "limit": 5, "include_schema": false}`. Each
match says whether the current profile shows it and, if not, which profile
does. Ask for schemas only for the tool you will call.

## 4. One snapshot, then compute

For any question about more than a few elements:

1. Call `snapshot_take` once. Scope it with `categories` on large models.
2. Answer with `snapshot_compute`: a pipeline of steps (join, where,
   group_by, aggregate, sort, select, limit) that returns only the result.
3. Reuse the same `snapshot_id` for follow-up questions. Take a new snapshot
   only after the model changed.

Use `snapshot_diff` to compare two snapshots. Do not read elements one at a
time with `revit_get_element_parameters` in a loop. The pipeline syntax is in
`docs/snapshot-compute.md`.

## 5. Ask for less

- On list reads such as `revit_list_elements`, pass `limit`, `offset` or
  `count_only`.
- Where the schema offers `response_options`, pass `fields` to keep only the
  paths you need. Read results are compact by default.
- In `snapshot_compute`, end with `select` and `limit`, and set `max_rows`.
- A result marked `truncated: true` was trimmed. Narrow the call; do not
  repeat it unchanged.

## 6. One plan per change set

When writes need a plan:

1. Collect every change for one purpose, then call `plan_actions` once with all
   actions. Do not make one plan per element.
2. Show the person the preview: elements, old values, new values, and the
   blast radius.
3. Stop. Ask the person to approve the plan in the AEC Bridge panel or with
   the `aec-model-bridge-approve` command. Never approve, reject or roll back a
   plan yourself. Those tools are not available to clients, and a call returns
   kind `human_only`.
4. After the person approves, call `execute_plan`. Use `list_pending_plans` to
   check plan state.
5. Confirm the change from the result, or read the values back. Never say a
   change was made until a result confirms it.

## 7. Read the error kind

A failed call returns `isError: true` and `structuredContent.error.kind`. A
module tool returns `ok: false` with `kind`, `message` and `hint`. Look the
kind up in `docs/error-catalogue.md`, which says when it happens and what to do.
The common ones:

- `approval_blocked`: no matching approved plan. Make a plan with
  `plan_actions` and ask the person to approve it. Do not retry unchanged.
- `tool_profile_blocked`: the profile hides the tool. Use a listed tool, or ask
  the person to switch the profile.
- `unknown_tool`: wrong name. Call `search_tools`.
- `bridge_error`: Revit is not reachable or the command failed. Call
  `revit_health` and tell the person.
- `human_only`: stop and ask the person.

## Install in other clients

The skill folder follows the Agent Skills format (a folder with `SKILL.md`).
Copy the `aec-model-bridge` folder:

- Claude Code: install the plugin with `/plugin marketplace add Sam-AEC/aec-model-bridge`
  and `/plugin install aec-model-bridge@aec-model-bridge`. The skill loads from
  the plugin. Or copy the folder to `.claude/skills/` in a project.
- Codex: copy the folder to `.agents/skills/` in the repository or to
  `~/.agents/skills/` for every repository. Older Codex docs name
  `.codex/skills/`. UNVERIFIED: check with `/skills` in Codex.
- Cursor: copy the folder to `.cursor/skills/` in the project. Cursor
  documents that it also reads `.claude/skills/` and `.codex/skills/`.
  UNVERIFIED in a live Cursor session.

=== FILE: docs/dev-workflow.md ===

# Branches and merging

How changes reach `main`, and the habits we keep to a minimum.

## The branches

| Branch | What it is | Who changes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `main` | What a release is cut from. Always passes CI. | Only through a pull request, never by a direct push. |
| `dev` | Where finished, green work is combined and tested by the owner before it goes to `main`. | Merge commits from reviewed branches. No force-push. |
| `feat/…`, `fix/…`, `docs/…` | One change each. | Anyone, through a pull request. |

## The path of a change

1. Work on a branch named for the change. One concern per branch.
2. Open one pull request. Describe what changed, how it was tested, and what is **UNVERIFIED** (anything that needs a real Revit).
3. CI (`ci-success`) must pass and review threads must be answered.
4. A green branch is merged into `dev` with a **merge commit**, not a squash. That keeps the commit ids, so GitHub marks the pull request as merged when `dev` later goes to `main`.
5. The owner tests `dev` on a real machine. When they are happy, `dev` goes to `main` in one pull request.

## Protecting `main`

The ruleset in [`.github/rulesets/protect-main.json`](../.github/rulesets/protect-main.json) blocks direct pushes, force-pushes and deletion of `main`, and requires:

- a pull request with one approving review (stale approvals are dismissed on push), merged with a merge commit,
- the `ci-success` check, on a branch that is up to date with `main`,
- every review thread resolved.

Repository admins can bypass the rules **only while merging a pull request**, not by pushing. [`protect-dev.json`](../.github/rulesets/protect-dev.json) stops `dev` being deleted or force-pushed and requires a pull request (squash merge) and the `ci-success` check. [`protect-tags.json`](../.github/rulesets/protect-tags.json) stops `v*` tags being created, moved or deleted except by repository admins. The files mirror the live rulesets; the `rulesets-drift` workflow compares them every week.

To apply them (the repository owner, in GitHub): **Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New ruleset → Import a ruleset**, choose each file, then check the preview and save. The import checks the schema and will say if a field is not accepted.

## Releases

Because direct pushes to `main` are blocked, a release is:

1. Open a pull request that bumps the version and changelog (`chore(release): X.Y.Z`).
2. Merge it when `ci-success` is green.
3. Tag the merge commit (`git tag vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z`). Pushing a tag is not blocked.

Nothing is published until the owner confirms a release.

## Habits we skip on purpose

- No direct commits to `main`, and no force-pushes anywhere.
- No squash merges into `dev`, because they hide which pull request a change came from.
- No hand-merging of generated files. `docs/tools-generated.md` is regenerated with `python scripts/generate_tool_docs.py`.
- No new tool, module or screen without a test that fails without it.
- No claim in the docs that has not been checked. Unchecked things are marked UNVERIFIED.
- No second pull request for the same change.

=== FILE: docs/record-replay.md ===

# Record and replay bridge sessions

The server can record the traffic between itself and the Revit add-in to a cassette file, and later serve those recorded responses without Revit. Use it to turn a live session into a regression test, or to reproduce a report without the original model.

## Record a session

Recording is off by default. It works only in bridge mode (`MCP_REVIT_MODE=bridge`). In mock mode the setting is ignored and a warning is logged.

```powershell
$env:MCP_REVIT_MODE = "bridge"
$env:MCP_REVIT_RECORD = "walls-check"
python -m revit_mcp_server
```

- `MCP_REVIT_RECORD` is a plain cassette name: letters, digits, `_` or `-`, at most 64 characters. The values `1`, `true`, `on` and `yes` pick a timestamped name such as `session-20261124-101500`.
- The cassette is written to `<workspace>/cassettes/<name>.jsonl`. The path is built with `safe_child`, so a name that is a path (`../x`, `C:\x`, `a/b`, `x.jsonl`) is refused. A refused name fails closed: every Revit call reports why, and nothing is sent to Revit unrecorded.
- Each bridge call is appended as one JSON line. Lines are added to an existing cassette of the same name.
- Calls routed by the panel hub to another Revit instance are recorded too.
- A failure to write the cassette (for example a full disk) is logged and does not fail the Revit call.
- Batches are off while recording. An approved plan runs one action at a time (no `revit.execute_plan_batch`, so no single undo step), and element reads are sent one command at a time (no `revit.batch`). Every write and read is then a line in the cassette, and replay serves it the same way.

### What is masked

Before a line is written:

- Secrets and tokens are replaced with `<redacted>`: values under keys such as `token`, `session_token`, `password`, `api_key`, `authorization`, `secret` and `code`, `token=...` text, and secret values registered by the process (such as the panel token).
- Local file paths (Windows drive paths, UNC shares, rooted and POSIX paths) are replaced with `<redacted-path>`.
- The local OS user name and email addresses are replaced with `<redacted-user>`, and so are the values of person fields such as `user`, `author`, `owner`, `created_by` and `last_saved_by`.

The live caller still gets the real, unmasked response. Only the cassette is masked.

### Review before sharing

A cassette from a real model can still contain model data: project and element names, parameter values, element ids, view and sheet names, family names and free text that the masking rules do not recognise. Masking is pattern-based and can miss a value. Open the file and review it before you share it, attach it to an issue or commit it.

## Cassette format

One JSON object per line:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seq` | Line number in recording order, starting at 1. |
| `v` | Cassette format version. This server reads version `1`. |
| `tool` | The MCP tool call that made this bridge request, when known. |
| `arguments` | The masked MCP tool arguments. |
| `arguments_redacted` | `true` when masking changed the arguments, so they may not replay at tool level. |
| `command` | The bridge command, such as `revit.list_levels`. `__get_result__` is a `revit_get_result` lookup. |
| `params` | The masked bridge parameters, without `request_id` and `wait_ms`. |
| `ok` | `true` for a response, `false` for an error. |
| `response` | The masked result, as the provider received it after unwrapping. |
| `error` | `{type, message, payload}` with `type` `CommandFailed` (Revit ran the command and it failed) or `BridgeError`. |

## Replay a cassette

```powershell
$env:MCP_REVIT_MODE = "replay"
$env:MCP_REVIT_CASSETTE = "C:\revit-workspace\cassettes\walls-check.jsonl"
python -m revit_mcp_server
```

- Replay never contacts Revit.
- A request matches a line on its command and its normalised parameters: masked the same way as when recording, `request_id` and `wait_ms` removed, key order ignored.
- Equal requests are served in recorded order. When they run out, the last one repeats.
